0JsPcm_Vl1g.plain_title: How JAX lets you write code once and transform it many ways
0JsPcm_Vl1g.big_question: Why do scientists and machine learning researchers choose JAX over other tools, and what does it actually do differently under the hood?
0JsPcm_Vl1g.everyday_anchor: Imagine you write a Python function that computes x squared. With JAX, you can instantly get a new function that computes the derivative (2x) without manually writing calculus. Better yet, you can take that derivative function and ask for its derivative too, or run your original function on thousands of examples in parallel automatically, or compile it to run 8x faster—all by adding one or two lines of code.
walkthrough: JAX is a Python library that does two fundamentally different things from most other tools. First, it makes matrix math and array operations blazingly fast by automatically sending them to GPUs (graphics processors) instead of CPUs. A 10,000 by 10,000 matrix multiply that takes 7 seconds on a normal computer takes 0.05 seconds on a GPU through JAX—126 times faster. This works because GPUs have thousands of tiny cores that can do the same operation on different pieces of data at the same time, whereas CPUs have only a handful of very fast cores designed for tasks that happen one after another. When you do machine learning or scientific computing, almost everything boils down to matrix operations, so GPUs are perfect.

But the truly revolutionary part of JAX is not the speed. It is something called program transformation, which is the idea that you can take a Python function and automatically rewrite it into a completely different function that does something mathematically related. The most famous example is automatic differentiation: you define a function f(x) that computes something (say, x squared). Then you write grad_f = jax.grad(f), and grad_f is now a brand new Python function that when you call grad_f(5), it returns the derivative of f at that point. The clever part: JAX didn't just memorize the rule that the derivative of x^2 is 2x. Instead, it actually rewrote your function into lower-level code, figured out the derivative using calculus rules (chain rule, product rule, etc.), and handed you back executable Python code that computes it.

What makes this effective is composability: you can chain transformations together. If you have grad_f, you can call jax.grad(grad_f) to get a function that computes the second derivative. You can keep going: third derivatives, fourth derivatives, as deep as you want. Each transformation takes the output of the previous one and transforms it further. This is hard in tools like PyTorch because PyTorch tracks gradients through specific numbers you give it (you compute f(5), then ask for the derivative at that value). JAX gives you the derivative as an actual reusable function. You can take it anywhere, call it at any point, compose it with other functions.

JAX implements this magic by treating your Python code as data. When you ask it to transform a function, JAX doesn't just run your function. It first converts it into an intermediate language (JAX's own low-level representation) that strips away Python specifics and exposes the raw mathematical operations—addition, multiplication, matrix multiplies, element-wise operations, etc. Then it applies the transformation to this intermediate code to produce a new intermediate program. Finally, it converts that back into executable Python. This is what we mean by metaprogramming: programs that write other programs.

A second effective transformation is vectorization (vmap). Suppose you write a function that takes one number x and computes x times a weight plus a bias. If you want to do this for 1,000 different x values (a batch), you would normally write a for loop. But that's slow in Python. Instead, you call jax.vmap(f), and it automatically rewrites your function so it accepts an array of x values and computes the result for all of them at once using matrix operations, which runs in parallel. JAX is smart enough to see that your scalar dot product can become a matrix multiply when the input has an extra dimension. You tell vmap which dimension of which argument contains the batch, and it figures out the rest.

A third transformation is compilation (jit, just-in-time). Your original function might call multiple operations: compute x squared, compute x cubed, add them together. Normally this means three separate jobs submitted to the GPU: one kernel (small program) computes squares, one computes cubes, one sums. Each kernel has to read data from GPU memory and write results back, and that read/write is the bottleneck. When you wrap your function in jax.jit, JAX's compiler (called XLA) notices it can fuse these three kernels into one: read x once, compute all three things in fast on-chip memory, write the result once. This can easily make code 8 times faster. The catch: compilation takes time (a few seconds) and only pays off if you call the function hundreds of times.

JAX makes these transformations composable and chainable, which is why it has become the tool of choice for research. You might vmap a function across a batch, then jit the result, then wrap the whole thing in grad to get gradients. You write the core logic once, and the transformations handle the parallelism, the acceleration, and the calculus. This is especially effective for scientific machine learning: you write the physics simulation (finite difference solver, ODE integrator) in a handful of lines of NumPy-like code. Then you can instantly ask for gradients through the entire simulation so you can optimize a parameter (like material properties) to match experimental data. You cannot do this easily in PyTorch because it wasn't designed for these kinds of intricate transformations and compositions.

The ecosystem around JAX is growing rapidly. Libraries like Optax provide off-the-shelf optimizers (Adam, SGD, etc.) so you don't write gradient descent by hand. Diffrax lets you train neural differential equations—neural networks that are built into physics equations. DeepXDE helps you solve physics-informed neural networks. JAX MD does molecular dynamics. The fact that JAX is built on composable transformations means that once you implement one new technique, you get automatic differentiation through it, automatic parallelization, automatic compilation, all for free. This is why AlphaFold (which predicts protein 3D structure), Gemini (Google's large language model), and cutting-edge climate simulation all use JAX.
key_ideas: Accelerated arrays: JAX uses XLA to compile Python array operations to run on GPUs, making matrix math 100+ times faster by exploiting GPU parallelism.
Program transformation: JAX can rewrite your Python functions into new functions that compute related quantities (derivatives, batches, compiled versions) without you having to rewrite the logic.
Automatic differentiation (grad): turns a function into a new function that computes its gradient using the chain rule, composable so you can take derivatives of derivatives.
Vectorization (vmap): turns a scalar function into a batched function that processes many examples in parallel using matrix operations instead of loops.
Just-in-time compilation (jit): rewrites your function to fuse operations and minimize GPU memory traffic, typically 5–8x speedup but with upfront compilation cost.
Composability: transformations can be chained together (grad ∘ vmap ∘ jit), so you write core logic once and get multiple capabilities automatically.
Functional purity: JAX functions should be stateless and deterministic; no hidden side effects means transformations can safely reorder and fuse operations.
0JsPcm_Vl1g.worked_intuition: Let's trace through a real example: linear regression with gradient descent. You write a forward function f(w, b, x) = w*x + b that takes weight w, bias b, and a single data point x, and returns a prediction. Then you vmap it: f_batch = vmap(f, in_axes=(None, None, 0)), meaning don't parallelize over w and b, but parallelize over x. Now f_batch(w, b, [x1, x2, x3]) returns [f(w,b,x1), f(w,b,x2), f(w,b,x3)] using a matrix multiply under the hood. Next, you define a loss function that calls f_batch, computes mean squared error. You ask for grad_loss = grad(loss_fn), which returns a function that computes dL/dw and dL/db. Then you compile the update step with jit. Now inside a for loop (which runs in Python, not JAX), you call the compiled jitted gradient update 1,000 times. The first call pays a 2-second compilation cost. The next 999 calls each take 1 millisecond because the GPU has a fused kernel ready. Total time: ~2 seconds for 1,000 steps. If you tried to do this naively in Python with explicit loops, it would take minutes.
0JsPcm_Vl1g.where_it_breaks: JAX has real constraints. First, your code must be pure: no print statements, no random number generation (you must pass a random key explicitly), no if/else based on data values (only on static shapes known at compile time). This is because JAX needs to trace through code to build its intermediate representation, and side effects break that. Second, compilation is expensive and happens on the first call with a given input shape; if your function changes size, it recompiles. Third, JAX arrays are immutable (you cannot modify in place), which is fine for numerical code but feels weird if you are used to NumPy in-place operations. Fourth, JAX is not a complete replacement for scientific computing libraries; some things from SciPy do not have JAX equivalents yet, so you may need to use multiple tools. Finally, the error messages can be cryptic because errors can happen deep in the compiled code, not in your original Python.
0JsPcm_Vl1g.takeaway: JAX's core insight is that mathematical transformations (differentiation, parallelization, compilation) can be implemented as code-to-code rewrites of functions, not as runtime tricks. This makes your code simpler, faster, and more composable. You write the math once, and JAX automatically gives you derivatives, parallelism, and GPU speed.

4c_efyhCaQs.plain_title: Why solving equations backwards—learning operators instead of solutions
4c_efyhCaQs.big_question: When you want to solve PDEs for many inputs, is it better to solve each one from scratch, or learn to recognize the pattern that maps inputs to outputs? And what does it even mean to do that with infinite-dimensional objects like functions?
4c_efyhCaQs.everyday_anchor: Imagine you're a weather forecaster. Every day you get a new map of today's temperatures and have to predict tomorrow's. Instead of running an expensive physics simulation each time, you watch a thousand past examples and learn to see the pattern yourself. That's operator learning—but mathematicians make it rigorous.
walkthrough: So far in this course, you've learned PINNs—physics-informed neural networks. They take the equation itself (like the Laplace equation) and use it as a teaching signal during training. You make guesses for the solution, compute the residual (how badly it violates the equation), and push that residual to zero. It's direct: equation-driven, no data needed. But it hits a wall when solutions have high frequencies or rapid changes—the training becomes exponentially harder because the optimization is poorly conditioned, like trying to solve a problem where the steepness of the landscape changes wildly. Preconditioning helps for simple 1D or 2D problems, but it barely dents the real issue.

The core limitation of PINNs is that they're glued to one question: 'Given this input (time, space, a source term), what is the solution *at this point*?' Mathematically, they're computing u(x,t) for fixed (x,t), point by point. But there's a richer way to think about PDEs. Most PDEs are systems: you give them an input (like a material property field or initial condition), and they produce an output (pressure field, velocity field). The relationship between inputs and outputs is deterministic and can be learned from data. This relationship is called a *solution operator*—a mapping from input functions to output functions. It's infinite-dimensional, because functions are infinite-dimensional (uncountably many points), but it encodes *system behavior*, not individual evaluations.

Here's a concrete example: subsurface flow (Darcy's law). The input is permeability—a spatially varying property of the rock. The output is pressure distribution. You could run an expensive finite element solver for each new permeability map, or you could gather data from many solves and train a network to recognize the mapping directly. Similarly, for compressible Euler equations in 2D, the input is an initial condition (density, velocity field), and the output is the solution at a later time. The operator maps the whole initial state to the whole later state. This is second-order thinking: not 'what's u at point x,' but 'what does this system do to this entire input function?'

Once you reframe the problem as operator learning, a natural question arises: can you just reduce it to finite dimensions? One naive answer is to parameterize your inputs. For airfoil design, instead of allowing arbitrary shapes, you fix a base shape and vary it using 20 basis functions (spline bumps). Now you have 20 parameters instead of a function. Train a network to map those 20 parameters to drag and lift. It works great—until someone needs 30 parameters to describe their design space. Your network, trained on 20 inputs, is useless. It doesn't generalize because even though shapes with 20 and 30 bumps might look visually similar, the parametrization doesn't respect that similarity. Parametrization is a strict jacket: it limits the space you can explore and kills generalization as soon as the parameters change.

So genuine operator learning must work with functions, not parameters. But you still need to use neural networks, which inherently work with finite-dimensional vectors. The solution is discretization: translate the infinite-dimensional problem into a finite-dimensional one in a way that respects the continuous structure. The simplest approach is 'discretize and learn.' You take your function input, sample it at a grid of points (say, 16 by 16 = 256 points in 2D). Pass those 256 numbers through an MLP. The MLP outputs 256 numbers (predictions at the same grid). Now you have a finite-dimensional map: R^256 to R^256, which you can train with standard neural networks.

But this 'discretize and learn' has three killer flaws. First: model size explodes. A 64-by-64 2D grid is 4,096 points. An MLP layer from 4,096 inputs to 4,096 outputs requires roughly 10-16 million parameters *for just one layer*. Move to 3D (64^3 = 262,000 points) and you need billions of parameters for a single layer. Your model becomes memory-prohibitive. Second: the points are treated as independent, losing spatial structure. Nearby grid points are highly correlated (smooth solutions vary slowly in space), but the MLP treats all 4,096 inputs as separate coordinates. This is wasteful and inefficient. Third, and most fundamentally: the network is bound to a fixed resolution. If you trained on 64-by-64 data, you can only evaluate on 64-by-64 data. Change to 128-by-128 and you can't use the network; the input dimension doesn't match. This isn't true operator learning, because a real operator doesn't care how finely you sample it—the underlying function-to-function mapping stays the same.

The resolution problem is the deepest issue. When you discretize to a grid and train on that grid, you're really learning a 'map from one specific discretization to another specific discretization.' If you refine the grid and add points between the old points, your network has no way to ingest that new information. You'd have to interpolate, but interpolation adds assumptions about what the function does between grid points—and that breaks the pure learning-from-data philosophy. Mathematically, the network is learning a map from R^n to R^n for a fixed n, not a genuine operator (which would be from function space to function space). You can change resolution in practice (by interpolating up or downsampling), but it requires post-processing tricks and isn't built into the architecture. Genuine operator learning means the model never 'sees' the points; it sees only functions and should work at any resolution automatically.

The next lectures will address this by building architectures that truly work on function spaces. Fourier neural operators encode functions as coefficients in a Fourier basis (infinite-dimensional), then apply learnable transformations in that basis, then decode back to function space. Graph neural operators discretize the domain into nodes but treat the discretization as incidental (a way to access the function), not fundamental. Attention-based operators learn position-invariant rules about how to process functions. These methods fix the resolution problem by building resolution-independence into the architecture itself. The goal is an operator learning approach where you can train on 64-by-64 data and confidently evaluate on 256-by-256 data, because you're truly learning the system's behavior, not memorizing a specific grid.
key_ideas: PDEs encode systems that map inputs to outputs—not individual points. Think of an operator as a function that eats a function and spits out a function, capturing how a system transforms entire fields.
PINNs solve equations point-by-point and struggle with high frequencies because training is ill-conditioned. Operator learning sidesteps this by learning from data instead of from residuals.
Parametrization (forcing infinite-dimensional inputs into 20 fixed parameters) seems like a shortcut but destroys generalization—as soon as your design space changes, the network becomes useless.

Discretization (sampling functions on a grid, training an MLP, interpolating the output) is simple but traps you: your network only knows the resolution it trained on, and changing grid size requires post-processing tricks, not genuine understanding.

True operator learning must be resolution-independent—the network should work automatically at any resolution because it learned the underlying function-to-function mapping, not a specific grid-to-grid mapping.
The cure requires new architectures (like Fourier neural operators) that work natively in function spaces and build resolution-invariance into the design, rather than bolting it on after the fact.

Infinite-dimensional thinking is hard with finite computers, but the key insight is this: you can discretize the learning process without discretizing the learning target—learn on discrete data without baking discretization into the model.
4c_efyhCaQs.worked_intuition: Picture a 1D function on the interval [0, 1]: it might start low, spike in the middle, and drop at the end. An operator G transforms it (say, via diffusion) to a smoother version. Now, the naive approach: sample the input at 5 points (say, at 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0), feed those 5 numbers to an MLP, get 5 output numbers, and interpolate. This works for that resolution. But what if you later want to sample the *same function* at 9 points (0, 0.125, 0.25, ...)? The 5-point MLP has no way to use the extra information in the two new points between the originals. It's bound to 5-point thinking. A true operator, though, would see 'this is a bump-shaped function' regardless of whether you describe it with 5 or 9 samples, because it's learning the smooth diffusion rule itself—spreading peaks outward smoothly—not a lookup table for a specific grid.
4c_efyhCaQs.where_it_breaks: Discretize-and-learn breaks when: (1) you need high resolution (billion-parameter networks become impractical), (2) you want to generalize to untrained resolutions (your test data at 256x256 can't feed into a model trained on 64x64), and (3) you're trying to work with 3D+time data (memory and compute explode). It also fails philosophically—it learns a particular grid, not the underlying operator. For truly intricate systems (high-dimensional, chaotic, or multiscale), you need a better path.
4c_efyhCaQs.takeaway: Operator learning is learning the pattern *'what does this system do to any function input?'* rather than *'what is the solution at this point?'* Discretize-and-learn shows why you can't just reduce to finite dimensions naively—you lose resolution generalization and explode in model size. The cure is to design networks that truly work in function spaces, so that learning is untethered from a particular grid. This is the hard problem the course tackles next.

5XaLKR08TwI.plain_title: How to make convolutions work for learning physics: convolutional neural operators
5XaLKR08TwI.big_question: Deep learning works amazingly well for images using convolutions, but when we try to learn solutions to physics problems (PDEs), convolutions fail: they don't preserve the mathematical structure we need. Can we fix convolutions so they work for physics?
5XaLKR08TwI.everyday_anchor: Imagine you have a recipe for making bread that works if your oven is exactly 400°F. But if the temperature changes, the recipe breaks—the bread turns out completely different. Now imagine a better recipe that works at ANY temperature, whether your oven is 350°F or 425°F. That's the difference: most neural networks fail when the grid resolution changes, but the method in this lecture works no matter what resolution you use.
walkthrough: The fundamental problem is this: physics is described by PDEs (partial differential equations)—mathematical rules that describe how things like temperature, pressure, or velocity change across space and time. To solve a PDE means to learn the operator—the mathematical machine that takes an input function (like initial pressure everywhere) and outputs an answer (like pressure at a later time everywhere). But this operator lives in infinite-dimensional function spaces, not in discrete grids. When you train a neural network on one grid resolution and test it on another, the whole thing breaks. The convolutions in standard CNNs (convolutional neural networks) were designed for images, and they silently assume the input lives on a particular discrete grid. If you change the grid, the math no longer works.

The key insight is to work with band-limited functions—functions that only contain frequencies up to some cutoff point. In the Fourier transform (a way to decompose any signal into pure frequencies), a band-limited function has zero energy above some frequency W. This matters because of the Nyquist theorem from signal processing: if your spacing between grid points is small enough (the Nyquist condition), then there is a perfect, one-to-one match between the continuous function and the discrete grid points. You can go from continuous to discrete and back without losing information. This is the bridge we'll use.

Here's the first fix for convolutions. Instead of treating the kernel (the filter we slide across the signal) as if it lives on a particular grid, we keep it discrete but act with it continuously. The convolution kernel is a sum of Dirac delta functions at fixed points. When we convolve with a band-limited function on a grid, we upsample the grid points to the continuous function (using sinc interpolation), apply the kernel at the original fixed points, and then resample back to the new grid. This way, the kernel stays fixed but the input functions are rescaled to match it. The operator commutes—you get the same answer whether you compute on a coarse grid, lift to continuous, resample to coarse, apply the kernel, or any other path through the diagram.

The second and trickier fix is for nonlinearities like ReLU. The problem: when you apply ReLU pointwise to a band-limited function, you create new high frequencies that weren't there before. This violates the band-limit assumption. The solution is surprisingly elegant: before applying the nonlinearity, upsample the function to a higher bandwidth (say, double the frequencies). This temporarily creates room for the new frequencies that the nonlinearity will generate. After the nonlinearity, use a low-pass filter to downsample back to the original bandwidth. The high-frequency noise created by the nonlinearity gets quenched. This process is non-local (it involves the entire continuous function, not just local points), but it preserves the structure needed to be a true neural operator.

For polynomial and rational nonlinearities, this is exact—you can compute exactly how much the bandwidth must grow (for squaring, double it; for fourth power, quadruple it). For smooth nonlinearities like ReLU or Swish, it's approximate, but the aliasing error is much smaller than if you didn't upsample. In practice, doubling the bandwidth is usually enough because the coefficients of very high frequencies naturally decay. The cost is real: you must evaluate the function at more grid points during the nonlinearity. But this is the price of keeping the structure.

A bare-bones architecture would just stack convolutions and these special nonlinearities. But from computer vision, we know you need more sophistication. Real systems have multi-scale structure: both coarse features (the outline of a face) and fine details (exact location of eyes). The Convolutional Neural Operator uses a U-Net-style architecture. You progressively downsample (coarsen the grid, add channels) through an encoder, process at the bottleneck, then progressively upsample through a decoder, with skip connections that pass information from the encoder to the decoder. Residual connections (shortcuts around processing blocks) help gradients flow and preserve high-frequency information. Each building block—downsampling, convolution, nonlinearity—is itself a neural operator, so composing them preserves the property.

Why does this work empirically? The Navier-Stokes equations are a great test: they describe fluid flow and are genuinely hard. When you train a standard CNN or FNO at 64×64 resolution and then test at 32×32, both fail in different ways: errors explode because the discrete assumptions break. DeepONet falls apart completely, learning nothing but the mean. FNO does better (4% error) but introduces aliasing artifacts—visible ringing in the solution. A U-Net without the upsampling/downsampling (which violates the structure) also shows aliasing. But the Convolutional Neural Operator, built to be a true neural operator, maintains accuracy and structure across different resolutions. When you look at error spectra, standard methods show corruption in high frequencies, while CNO stays clean near machine precision.

The theoretical foundation is that neural operators can universally approximate operators, just as neural networks approximate functions. If an operator is continuous (small input changes yield small output changes), then a sufficiently large CNO can approximate it to arbitrary accuracy. This works because band-limited functions form a complete space for representing PDEs, and you can apply the universal approximation theorem to finite-dimensional neural networks within that space, then project back. You gain one level of abstraction—from approximating functions to approximating the infinite-dimensional mappings between them—but the principle is identical.
key_ideas: Band-limited functions are the secret: restrict to functions with frequencies up to some cutoff. This creates a one-to-one correspondence between continuous functions and discrete grid points (if grid is fine enough). No aliasing, perfect information transfer.

Fix convolutions by keeping the kernel fixed and resampling the input. The kernel lives at fixed locations. When the grid resolution changes, you resample the input function to match the kernel's reference points, apply the convolution, then resample back. The operator commutes—structure is preserved.

Fix nonlinearities with upsampling and downsampling. Before applying ReLU or other activations, allow higher frequencies (upsample). The nonlinearity can then create new frequencies safely. After, low-pass filter (downsample) back to the original bandwidth. This way, the created high frequencies don't corrupt the result.

True neural operators must satisfy continuous-discrete equivalence: the diagram where you go continuous→discrete→operate→discrete→continuous must commute. Polynomial and rational nonlinearities satisfy this exactly. Smooth nonlinearities (ReLU, Swish) satisfy it approximately but well enough to reduce aliasing dramatically.

Multi-scale processing is essential. Use a U-Net architecture: encoder (downsample while adding channels), bottleneck, decoder (upsample while removing channels). Process coarse and fine features at their own scales. Skip connections and residual shortcuts prevent gradient problems and preserve high-frequency information.

Empirical proof: train on one grid resolution, test on another. Standard CNNs and FNOs fail (errors explode, aliasing appears). Convolutional Neural Operators maintain accuracy and clean spectra, proving they are true neural operators—they work on any resolution.

Universal approximation for operators: any continuous operator between function spaces can be approximated to arbitrary accuracy by a neural operator, given enough parameters. This lifts the function approximation theorem to the operator level.
5XaLKR08TwI.worked_intuition: Let's work through the Navier-Stokes example concretely. You have a velocity field (how fast fluid is moving at each point) at time zero. A convolution alone preserves the band limit—if your input is band-limited, the output is too (because convolution with a discrete kernel preserves that property). But then you apply ReLU (set negative values to zero). This is a nonlinearity. A smooth curve becoming piecewise linear—this creates high-frequency Fourier components out of nowhere. If you didn't prepare for it, these frequencies alias (wrap around and corrupt the low frequencies). Solution: before ReLU, you upsample from say 4 frequencies to 8 frequencies. This is automatic in the continuous picture—you're just evaluating the sinc-interpolated function at more points. ReLU now acts on these 8-frequency values. Some values become zero, some stay positive. The new signal now has up to 16 frequencies (by the squaring property of frequency growth). You downsample back to 4 frequencies using sinc again (keeping the important low frequencies, throwing away high noise). The network has learned to manage frequency growth on its own. When you change the grid resolution (coarser or finer), this process scales automatically—the sinc interpolation adapts. That's why it's a true neural operator.
5XaLKR08TwI.where_it_breaks: The method has real limits. First, computational cost: upsampling multiplies grid points by 2, 4, or more. A 1024×1024 image becomes expensive fast. Second, the approximation for non-polynomial nonlinearities (like ReLU) is approximate, not exact. You lose some information when you downsample, and that error accumulates through layers. For highly oscillatory solutions (signals with very sharp features at very high frequencies), the assumption that band-limited functions capture the problem breaks down. Third, the architecture requires significant hyperparameter tuning: what bandwidth multiplier? How many U-Net levels? How many channels? Too few parameters and you can't learn the problem; too many and you overfit and burn compute. Finally, the theory guarantees universal approximation only with infinite layers and parameters; in practice, you're always approximating an approximation.
5XaLKR08TwI.takeaway: The insight is not that convolutions are bad—they're actually crucial for preserving locality and efficiency. The insight is that you must be honest about what space you're working in. If you pretend a discrete grid IS a continuous function and treat it that way, you fail when grids change. Instead, explicitly work with band-limited functions where discrete and continuous are equivalent. Keep kernels fixed and resample inputs. Manage frequency growth explicitly during nonlinearities. Build multi-scale architectures to handle different structural scales. When you do this, you get neural operators: networks that work on any resolution, any grid, any discretization—they learn the underlying continuous physics, not the grid.

5Y0sS-xqOAI.plain_title: Learning operators with transformers: using attention to solve PDEs
5Y0sS-xqOAI.big_question: How do we scale up neural networks to learn mathematical operators for PDEs when simpler convolutional architectures hit data-efficiency walls? What special trick lets transformers work on 2D and 3D problems despite their expensive all-to-all computations?
5Y0sS-xqOAI.everyday_anchor: Imagine you're trying to teach a neural network to predict how heat spreads through a material. You need thousands of training simulations—each one costing real money. Then someone invents a better "brain" (transformer with attention) that learns from fewer examples. But this brain is also expensive to run. The lecture shows you what attention does, why it works, and how to make it practical.
walkthrough: We start with a scaling problem: neural networks for PDEs (equations of physics) follow a known rule. Their error gets smaller as we add more training data, but only slowly—like the square root of the amount of data. This is actually a law of nature called the central limit theorem, not a bug we can fix. To get 1% error, you need roughly 10,000 samples. For expensive physics simulations, that's often $10 million to $30 million just to generate training data. This is why we need smarter architectures.

Previous architectures (FNO and CNO) use convolution—a local operation that mixes information from nearby points. They work reasonably well but all pay the same price for data. The question becomes: can we change the constants (make them better) rather than change the fundamental scaling rate? The answer comes from language models: they switched from RNNs to transformers and got a 5x efficiency gain on the same data-scaling curve.

Enter attention, the core of transformers. At each point in space, we want to update its value by collecting information from all other points. Unlike convolution, attention gathers signal from everywhere, but it's smart about which parts matter. For a point at location x, we compute 'weights' between it and every other point y: we transform each point's features through learnable matrices (called Query and Key), compute their similarity, apply softmax to turn it into a probability-like weight, and use those weights to aggregate values. This is a nonlinear kernel—it depends on the actual data values, not just distances.

The brilliance is that this weighting is computed via a soft softmax operation that turns dot products between transformed features into a valid probability distribution. We then take a weighted average of transformed values (through another learnable matrix, the Value matrix). All the learnable pieces—Query, Key, Value, Output matrices—are applied pointwise; they don't mix information spatially themselves. Only the weighting part (computed from comparing queries to keys) creates global coupling. Multi-head attention just runs this computation multiple times with different learnable parameters and concatenates the results.

Transformers aren't just attention, though. Attention alone is a gentle nonlinearity (softmax just normalizes). To approximate arbitrary operators, we also need strong pointwise nonlinearities. This comes from a feed-forward network (MLP) applied at every point: linear transformation to hidden features, activation function like ReLU, then back to the original dimension. Stacking attention and MLP blocks with layer normalization and skip connections gives universal approximation power. One transformer block does: layer norm → multi-head attention → skip connection → layer norm → MLP → skip connection. Stack many blocks.

There's a critical catch: transformers are permutation-invariant. If you shuffle the spatial order of all your points, the output doesn't change—because softmax over all pairs and summation don't care about order. But physics and images do care about position. If you shuffle all pixels in an image, the picture looks like chaos, not a rearrangement of the same image. So we need positional encodings: learnable vectors (or fixed sinusoidal patterns) that tell the network 'this is point number 47' or 'this point is 5 units from the reference'. These are added to each point's input before processing. Now the network knows where it is.

The final scaling problem: attention costs order of K-squared in compute, where K is the number of points. For 1D with 100 points, that's 10,000 ops per block—fine. For 2D (100×100 = 10,000 points), it's 100 million per block. For 3D (100×100×100 = 1 million points), it's a trillion—infeasible. The solution is learned local averaging via patching (also called patchification). Instead of attending to every point, divide the domain into patches (small cells), compute a weighted average over each patch to create one representative token, then run attention on the K/P-squared tokens, where P is patch size. A 100×100 image with 10×10 patches becomes 100 tokens; attention now costs only 10,000 ops. The trick is that patches compress information lossily but acceptably for many problems.

This patching strategy is the vision transformer design: input → patch embeddings (learned local averages with position info for each patch) → transformer blocks → output. The accuracy-vs-compute tradeoff is real: large patches reduce compute but lose fine detail; small patches preserve detail but blow up compute. Most practitioners find 8×8 patches the practical sweet spot for many PDE problems. In 3D, this becomes more delicate, but the idea stands: compress via learned aggregation, then use transformer attention on the compressed representation. The entire lecture builds to this: data-efficient learning via nonlinear weighting (attention) made practical via spatial compression (patching).
key_ideas: Operator learning via neural networks hits a square-root data-scaling wall (from probability theory), not improvable in general; we improve the constant instead.
Attention is a data-dependent nonlinear kernel integral operator: it aggregates information from all points, but the weights depend on feature similarity, not just spatial distance.
Softmax normalizes the weights to probabilities; pointwise MLPs provide universal approximation; layer norms and skip connections stabilize training.
Transformers are permutation-invariant by design, so positional encodings (learnable position indicators) are essential to tell the network where each point is.
Direct attention on dense grids is computationally infeasible in 2D+ (O(K²) difficulty), but patching (learned local averaging + coarse attention on patch tokens) makes it practical.

Vision transformers compress spatial detail via patches, reducing token count; you trade detail loss for compute. The patch size is the main dial: bigger patches → faster but less accurate; smaller patches → slower but finer.
The entire architecture (attention + MLP + norms + patches) is resolution-agnostic: a model trained on coarse grids can be applied to fine grids by recomputing patch embeddings on the new grid.
5Y0sS-xqOAI.worked_intuition: Consider a simple 1D PDE: heat equation. You have 100 points in space. A FNO would convolve with neighbors (e.g., 5 points left/right). An attention-based operator computes, for every point i, a softmax-weighted sum of transformed values from all 100 points. The weights are learned: maybe point 47's value should strongly influence point 12 because they have correlated features, even if they're far apart. For a 1D sequence of 100 points, computing all pairwise similarities costs ~100×100 = 10K operations—very manageable. Now imagine a 2D air-temperature field on a 100×100 grid. Attention naively wants ~(10K)² = 100M ops. Instead, group the grid into 10×10 patches (100 patches total). For each patch, learn a weighted average of the 100 pixel values inside, producing a single token. Now apply attention to 100 tokens: ~100² = 10K ops again—feasible. You lose the ability to distinguish fine structure within patches, but for many PDE problems (especially coarse-grained ones), that detail isn't critical. If the ground-truth solution changes slowly spatially, patches capture it. If it has sharp corners at the pixel scale, patching fails.
5Y0sS-xqOAI.where_it_breaks: The approach breaks when you need fine spatial resolution AND the physics cares about fine detail. High-frequency phenomena (sharp shocks, turbulence micro-scales) are averaged away by patching. On small domains or for 1D problems, patching offers no speedup and only loses information, so you'd use direct attention instead. Permutation-invariance (before positional encodings) means the raw attention mechanism cannot distinguish spatial structure; positional encodings are not learned automatically—they must be provided explicitly. With very small patch sizes (e.g., 2×2) in 3D, you're back to O(K²) difficulty. There's no universal patch size: a 16×16 patch works for low-resolution images but loses too much structure for high-resolution scientific data. Finally, vision transformers still require many samples to train well compared to, say, classical PDE solvers with physics constraints built in.
5Y0sS-xqOAI.takeaway: Transformers learn flexible, nonlinear operators via attention (all-to-all weighting of features), but the O(K²) cost is only practical with spatial compression (patching). Larger patches = faster, but less accurate. Smaller patches = slower, but finer. The choice of patch size is the critical dial balancing compute against information loss.

6qT7k3WMUoo.plain_title: When neural networks fail at turbulence: why generative models are the answer
6qT7k3WMUoo.big_question: Why do standard neural operators completely fail at predicting turbulent flows even with thousands of training examples, and what fundamentally different approach actually works?
6qT7k3WMUoo.everyday_anchor: Imagine you're trying to predict exactly where a leaf will land as it falls through turbulent air. Two tiny changes to where you release it lead to completely different paths—the tiniest variations explode into massive differences. That is what makes turbulent flows chaotic, and it is why a neural network trained to predict individual outcomes will fail catastrophically.
walkthrough: For most of this course, neural operators have been wildly successful—they learn to predict smooth solutions to physics equations from data, catching intricate behaviors that humans would struggle to code by hand. But we hit a hard wall: turbulent fluid flows. These are dominated by two properties that break everything we built. First, multiscale structure—the solution contains eddies and vortices at wildly different sizes, from large swirling patterns down to tiny threads. Second, chaos—if you change the initial condition by less than one percent, the solution diverges by nearly one hundred percent. These two properties are linked: chaos creates the multiscale chaos, which feeds back into chaos, creating an inescapable tangle.

The problem is not architectural or a lack of data. The lecturer trained a hybrid neural operator on Navier-Stokes equations starting from simple initial conditions (Taylor-Green vortex), using thousands of high-resolution simulations. The result: order-of-one errors, and worse, the network predicts only the average, washing out every small-scale structure. When you give it slightly perturbed initial conditions that should produce wildly different outputs, it outputs almost the same thing. The network is blind to the perturbations because it has learned to be insensitive to tiny changes—and that is a fundamental feature, not a bug.

Why is neural insensitivity inevitable? During training, gradient descent requires bounded gradients to move smoothly through weight space. If gradients exploded, training would fail. This forces the network to be Lipschitz continuous—meaning the output cannot change too much when the input changes slightly. Formally, the Lipschitz constant bounds how much the output can change per unit input change. For a trained neural network, this constant is necessarily of order one or modest (maybe 10, maybe 0.5), never a million. In a chaotic system, the ground truth solution map has unbounded Lipschitz constant—tiny perturbations grow to huge outputs. The neural network physically cannot learn this behavior.

A clever mathematical decomposition makes this crystal clear. When you perturb the input by a tiny amount and take the expectation of the output error, you can split it into two pieces: the bias term (what the network outputs when it cannot distinguish the perturbation) and the variance term (the actual variation in the ground truth output given different perturbations). The variance term is independent of the network—it is pure physics—and for chaos it is order one. The bias term, no matter how well trained, can only shrink to zero in the best case. Even zero bias is not enough: the ground truth variance dominates, so the network's prediction error floors at order one. In short, the network can only learn the mean, never the spreading caused by sensitivity.

The mean is not a useless target—it is what you should compute next. Because deterministic pointwise prediction is mathematically impossible for chaotic systems, the insight is to stop trying. Instead, give up on matching every vortex, every eddy, every filament. Instead, learn the probability distribution of solutions. This is statistical solution theory: you cannot guarantee where every eddy will be, but you can characterize what states are likely, what the average field looks like, what the variance looks like. If you have a probability distribution of initial conditions (even a narrow one from measurement uncertainty), you can evolve that distribution forward in time and ask the neural network to learn the conditional distribution—the distribution of outputs given inputs, not the deterministic map.

Generative models do exactly this. Instead of learning a function, learn a way to sample from a distribution. The key idea comes from diffusion: start with a known, simple distribution (standard Gaussian noise) and learn how to smoothly transform it into your target distribution (solutions of the PDE). During training, you go forward: take a real solution, add noise iteratively until it becomes pure Gaussian. During inference, you reverse: start with Gaussian noise, iteratively remove noise while conditioning on the initial conditions, and out pops a sample from the learned distribution of solutions. The noising and denoising are reversals of each other, linked by a stochastic differential equation that can be inverted mathematically.

The training algorithm is simple: given clean samples from your data, add Gaussian noise at various noise levels, then train a neural network (the denoiser) to predict the clean sample from the noisy version. This is just regression—standard supervised learning. Once trained, the denoiser is plugged into a formula (Tweedies formula, from probability theory) that approximates the score function—the log-gradient of the probability density. Solving the reverse stochastic differential equation with the score function iteratively at inference time creates samples from the target distribution. The beauty is that diffusion models work precisely because they do not need insensitive networks to learn chaos; they need the network to be a good denoiser at different noise levels, and denoising is learnable.

In practice for fluids, the architecture is a hybrid of convolutions (for local structure) and attention layers (for global relationships), trained to denoise velocity fields conditioned on initial conditions and prediction time. At inference, you sample Gaussian noise, feed it through the reverse SDE with the trained denoiser, and get out a plausible velocity field. Each sample is different (capturing uncertainty), but statistically correct (the ensemble of samples has the right statistics). This trades pointwise precision for distributional honesty—you cannot predict which microeddy will form where, but you can predict the probability that there will be a microeddy and its typical strength.
key_ideas: Chaos kills networks: tiny input changes explode to huge output changes, but trained networks must keep gradients bounded, making them insensitive to small perturbations. This is not fixable by architecture or data.

The Lipschitz trap: any network learned via gradient descent has a bounded Lipschitz constant, so it cannot match maps with unbounded sensitivity. The ground truth has unbounded sensitivity; the neural network cannot.

Multiscale structure lives in the variance: the mean of a chaotic ensemble washes out small scales; only the variance (the spread from tiny perturbations) contains the small eddies and filaments. Networks learn only the mean, never the variance.

Statistical solutions are the only honest target: instead of predicting where each vortex will be, predict the probability distribution of vortex positions and strengths. This trades deterministic precision for statistical correctness—the honest answer for chaos.

Diffusion models learn distributions by noising and denoising: iteratively add noise to data (forward process) then train a network to reverse it (backward process). The backward process is conditioned on the initial state, producing ensemble predictions with proper uncertainty.

Denoising is learnable, chaos is not: while chaotic dynamics are unlearnable in the pointwise sense, denoising noisy data at each noise level is straightforward supervised learning. This is why diffusion succeeds where standard neural operators fail.

Conditionality comes free: the initial conditions can be built into the denoiser as an additional input. At inference, samples from Gaussian noise conditioned on initial state automatically produce physically plausible solutions.
6qT7k3WMUoo.worked_intuition: Consider the Taylor-Green vortex (smooth sinusoid initial conditions). At time t=2, a standard neural operator trained on thousands of high-resolution simulations outputs something almost homogeneous—all the detail is gone. But if you run the true equations with a tiny 1% perturbation to the initial condition, you get a wildly different state (100% pointwise difference). The network saw this difference in training and learned to ignore it (because keeping it would require unbounded gradients). The true system is sensitive; the network learned to be insensitive. Now imagine instead of asking the network for one prediction, you ask it to generate random samples from the conditional distribution of solutions given initial conditions. Use diffusion: add noise to the initial condition, train a vision transformer to denoise it at different noise levels, then reverse the process at inference. Each sample is different (capturing chaos), but the ensemble of many samples has the right mean, variance, and small-scale structure. You have traded the impossible (one correct prediction) for the possible (statistically honest ensemble).
6qT7k3WMUoo.where_it_breaks: Diffusion models are computationally expensive—you must run the denoiser many times per sample (typically 50-1000 steps), making inference slow compared to a single forward pass through a standard neural operator. They also require matching the learned ensemble statistics to ground truth, which needs many samples and careful validation. For very short times (under one convective time scale), the chaos has not yet grown, so standard neural operators work fine; diffusion is overkill. The method assumes you can generate or access training data in the form of solution samples at various times—it does not work for entirely new physics without retraining.
6qT7k3WMUoo.takeaway: Chaotic systems with multiscale structure are unlearnable as deterministic maps because the neural network must have bounded gradients but the truth has unbounded sensitivity. The solution is to stop trying to predict individual outcomes and instead learn to sample from the distribution of outcomes using diffusion models. Train a denoiser, reverse the noising process at inference, and you get ensemble predictions with the right statistics—honest uncertainty quantification for a fundamentally unpredictable system.

9ETsTc5dhM8.plain_title: Learning operators on irregular point clouds with graphs and transformers
9ETsTc5dhM8.big_question: How do we teach neural networks to solve PDEs on real-world unstructured geometries and point clouds instead of just rectangular grids?
9ETsTc5dhM8.everyday_anchor: When you predict weather on Earth (which is a sphere) or simulate air flowing around an airplane wing (with its irregular bumpy shape), you cannot use a regular square grid. The world is made of scattered points. The lecture shows two ways to teach machines to learn from that messy reality.
walkthrough: For most of this course we have been working with PDEs on nice rectangular grids—Cartesian grids where all points sit in neat rows and columns. This works great for simple problems, but real engineering lives elsewhere. An airplane wing, a car body, the surface of Earth—none of these fit neatly on a grid. Instead they are described by irregular point clouds or unstructured meshes: thousands of points scattered wherever they are needed most (dense near sharp features, sparse far away). The question is: how do we teach a neural network (a learnable function approximator) to operate on this kind of data?

The first tool is called a graph neural network (GNN). A graph is just a collection of nodes (points) with edges (connections) between nearby nodes. If two points are neighbors, there is an edge linking them. The key insight is message passing: to update a point's information, you collect messages from all its neighbors, process them together, and compute a new value. This is done in layers, so information propagates: in layer one, a point learns from its direct neighbors; in layer two, it has heard from neighbors of neighbors, and so on. It is like whispering around a room—the farther you are from a speaker, the longer it takes for information to reach you. Graph neural networks are accurate because they respect locality (nearby points matter most) and adapt naturally to any shape.

But there is a catch: message passing on large point clouds is slow on modern computers. If you have 50,000 points, you must process millions of sparse memory accesses. Each point talks to its neighbors, and this creates random access patterns that GPUs dislike. One real example: training a 2D problem with 10,000 points took over two days. A 3D industrial problem with millions of points would be impossible. We need accuracy without sacrificing efficiency.

The answer is Geometry-Aware Operator Transformer (GOAT), which cleverly combines both worlds. The core idea: do not process the full messy point cloud directly. Instead, convert it into a simpler latent grid (either a regular Cartesian grid or a coarse subsampled point cloud) using an encoder. The encoder is a lightweight layer that says: 'for each red latent point, look at the nearby blue input points, gather information about them and their geometry, and summarize it.' This respects locality without message-passing overhead. Then, with the information now on a simpler grid, you can use a transformer (which is highly optimized on modern GPUs). Finally, a decoder reverses the process: given output on the latent grid, interpolate back to any query point you want.

What makes the encoder smart is multiscale aggregation. Instead of just looking at the nearest neighbors of a latent point, you look at neighbors at multiple distances: close neighbors, medium-range neighbors, far neighbors. You learn different weightings for each scale with attention (learned weights that depend on the data). You also encode geometric information: how many neighbors, how densely packed are they, how far from a boundary, what is the local shape. All of this goes into learned embeddings. The transformer then processes this rich information efficiently on the latent grid, where you can use standard vision transformers (very fast on GPUs).

The decoder mirrors the encoder's multiscale structure in reverse. When you want a solution at a new query point (say, one of your original input points), you look at all nearby latent grid points, gather their information at multiple scales, embed the geometry, and decode to get your answer. Because this is a neural field (a learned function defined everywhere), you can query any point you want, not just the training points. This is crucial for operator learning, where inputs and outputs are entire functions, and you want to evaluate them at any resolution.

Why does this work? The latent grid is the bottleneck. If you use a Cartesian latent grid and patch it (break it into small regions), the transformer processes patches super fast because modern GPUs are built for this. If you keep some sparsity and use attention, you still win: the bulk of compute (the transformer) is on a well-behaved grid; only the encoder and decoder (which are lightweight) touch the messy original geometry. The radios numbers are stunning: where graph networks process 10 samples per second on 50,000-point problems, GOAT processes 80 samples per second—10 times faster while staying accurate.

The method is flexible: it works on any domain geometry (airfoil, ball, deformable bodies, waves on circles, brain-shaped objects). The geometry information is baked into tokens via embeddings and attention. Because encoding and decoding are local operations with learned kernels and attention, not strict message passing, they scale much better. The processor (transformer) is plug-and-play: you could swap in FNO, CNN, or another architecture. The key innovation is that multiscale, geometry-aware encoder-decoder setup that moves heavy computation off the sparse graph and onto an efficient grid-based processor. It is a practical answer to the real-world constraint: you need accuracy on irregular geometries, but modern hardware loves grids.
key_ideas: Graph neural networks learn by message-passing: each point collects and processes information from neighbors in layers, but this is slow and memory-inefficient on large point clouds because of sparse, unpredictable memory access patterns.

A latent grid is a coarser, simpler representation (either a regular grid or subsampled points) onto which you map the original irregular input, encode geometry and features, process efficiently, then decode back to any query point.

Multiscale aggregation gathers information about each point at multiple neighborhood radii (close, medium, far), learns different weights for each scale via attention, and encodes rich geometric statistics (density, anisotropy, boundaries) as embeddings.

Geometry-aware tokens sit on a latent grid and contain physical features, geometric information (how far from boundary, how densely packed), and global field statistics. These can be processed by a transformer, which is highly optimized on modern GPUs.

The encoder-decoder approach separates concerns: lightweight encoder/decoder handle irregular geometry via local kernels and attention; heavy transformer processor handles the latent grid where GPUs excel; the result is 10x speedup with similar accuracy.

The method is a neural field (can evaluate output at any query point, not just training points), which respects the operator-learning principle that inputs and outputs are functions, not just fixed-resolution arrays.
9ETsTc5dhM8.worked_intuition: Imagine you have velocity (flow speed) measured at scattered points around an airplane. You want to predict how that flow evolves. A graph network would have each point whisper its velocity to neighbors, then neighbors pass messages again, layer by layer—accurate but slow. GOAT instead projects all that scattered data onto a coarse Cartesian grid (like a checkerboard with squares of a certain size). At each grid square, it asks: which input points fall near here? What is their average velocity? How clustered are they? Is it dense near the wing and sparse far away? It learns an embedding of this geometry and the velocity field. Now you have a simple grid, so you feed it to a transformer (which runs fast). The transformer processes it like an image. Then to get your answer at any original point, you interpolate from the processed grid, again using geometry-aware attention to decide which processed grid points matter most. The speedup comes from moving the expensive part (full message passing) to the inexpensive part (grid-based transformers).
9ETsTc5dhM8.where_it_breaks: The method trades some accuracy for speed. While GOAT is very accurate (1–3% error on many benchmarks), pure graph networks (RIGNO) are sometimes slightly more accurate on specific problems because they process every original point directly. For very irregular geometries with extreme anisotropy (vastly different point densities), the choice of latent grid strategy matters; a Cartesian grid wastes compute on empty space, while a subsampled latent point cloud loses expressivity. If you have billions of points (not millions), even GOAT may strain. The method assumes you can build a meaningful latent grid or subsample; for data with no clear structure, this can be awkward. Also, the attention mechanism in the encoder is data-dependent, so if neighbors change between samples, you recompute it each time (unlike fixed graph structures). Finally, the trick of using a Cartesian latent grid only works well if the underlying physics fits a grid; some problems (e.g., on highly curved manifolds) benefit from avoiding grids entirely.
9ETsTc5dhM8.takeaway: To solve PDEs on real irregular geometries efficiently, do not process the full messy point cloud with message-passing. Instead, map it to a simpler latent grid using a lightweight, multiscale, geometry-aware encoder; process the latent grid with a transformer (which GPUs love); then decode back to any query point. This achieves the accuracy of graph networks (respects locality and geometry) without the speed penalty (because the bottleneck processor runs on a well-structured grid). It is a practical reminder that machine learning on irregular domains is not just about better architectures—it is about smart problem reformulation.

AaChPylEH6U.plain_title: Why Physics-Informed Neural Networks Work (and When They Don't)
AaChPylEH6U.big_question: We can train neural networks to solve equations from physics without any examples of correct answers. How is this even possible, and what mathematical conditions have to be true for it to work?
AaChPylEH6U.everyday_anchor: Imagine you have a rule that heat spreads through materials. You know the rule perfectly (the math equation). You don't know what the answer looks like, but you can check whether any guessed answer obeys the rule. A neural network can learn by repeatedly guessing answers, checking how badly they break the rule, and fixing itself—like a student improving a solution by checking their work against a known constraint.
walkthrough: To understand how this works, we need to see the problem clearly. When you have a physics equation (a partial differential equation, or PDE), you're really asking: given some inputs F, find the solution U that satisfies the equation. The equation itself is written as D of U equals F, where D is a differential operator—basically a recipe for transforming U using calculus. For instance, the heat equation says that how temperature changes over time, plus how it spreads in space, equals the heat source. The solution U (the temperature field) has to satisfy this relationship everywhere in the domain.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) take a completely different approach from typical machine learning. They don't need labeled examples of correct answers. Instead, they use the equation itself as a teacher. Here's the mechanism: you train a neural network to output a guess for U at any location. Then, you automatically differentiate this neural network to compute what D of U would be at those locations. You compare D of U (from the network's guess) against F (which you know), and measure how far apart they are. This mismatch is called the residual—it tells you how badly the network's guess violates the equation. The training goal is to make the residual as small as possible everywhere. When the residual is near zero, the network's output approximately satisfies the physics.

But here's a tricky question: does minimizing the residual actually guarantee that your neural network's output is close to the true solution? Not automatically. This is where we need a bridge—a mathematical argument that connects 'the equation is nearly satisfied' to 'the answer is nearly correct.' The bridge is built on a property of PDEs called coercivity (or stability). This property says something intuitive: if two different inputs to a PDE are very close to each other, then their solutions must also be close. More formally, coercivity gives you a bound: the difference between two solutions is proportional to the difference between the inputs that created them. In other words, the PDE doesn't amplify small perturbations wildly—it behaves in a stable, controlled way.

Now apply this to your PINN. Your network solves a perturbed equation: instead of D of U equals F, it actually solves D of U_network equals F plus the residual error. The residual is like a small change to the input F. By the stability property, if the residual is small, then the output U_network must be close to the true solution U. This is the key mathematical link: small residual implies small error. This works not just for simple linear equations but also for nonlinear ones, though nonlinear cases introduce extra constants that depend on the specific solution.

But there's another gap. In practice, you can't compute the integral of the residual over the entire domain by hand. You sample the equation at random points in the domain, compute the residual at those points, and average them. This is called a quadrature—a numerical approximation of an integral. Here's the good news: if the underlying residual function is smooth (which it is, because the PDE solution is smooth), then as you add more quadrature points, the approximation converges to the true integral. So, making your training loss small (which is based on sampled points) pushes the true integral of the residual toward zero, which then pushes the actual error toward zero through the stability property.

The whole argument rests on whether neural networks can actually approximate smooth solutions well enough. This is where the universal approximation theorem comes in—a fundamental result saying that neural networks can approximate any continuous or integrable function arbitrarily well. But PINNs need more than that: they need the network and all its derivatives to approximate the solution and its derivatives well, because the residual involves derivatives. Fortunately, there are related theorems (including results by the lecturer) proving that neural networks can do this—they can approximate smooth functions along with their first, second, and higher-order derivatives. This completes the theoretical foundation: neural networks exist that can make both the training loss and the residual small simultaneously.

Finally, we have to ensure the problem is even solvable in practice—that we're not searching for a needle in a haystack. The existence results above prove that neural networks have the capacity to work, but they don't guarantee that gradient descent starting from a random initialization will find them. That's a separate, harder question about optimization. However, what we can say is: if there were a good solution out there (mathematically speaking, it should exist), then the loss landscape has a good point to find. This means the problem is 'well-posed' in the sense that we're not trying to accomplish something impossible.

In summary, PINNs work through a chain of logic: (1) Neural networks can approximate any smooth function and its derivatives arbitrarily well. (2) If a neural network approximates the true solution well, then the residual (the degree to which it violates the equation) becomes small. (3) If the residual is small and you have enough quadrature points, the training loss becomes small. (4) If the training loss is small and the PDE is stable (coercive), then the network's output must be close to the true solution. This creates a cycle: training to minimize a computable quantity (training loss) is equivalent to minimizing an uncomputable quantity (true error in solution space). But this chain can break at any link—if the PDE lacks stability, if the network can't be trained well, or if there aren't enough quadrature points, then the whole apparatus fails.
key_ideas: Residual: the mismatch between what a network predicts when you apply the equation to it, versus what the equation says should happen. Making residuals small is the entire goal of PINN training.

Coercivity (stability): a mathematical property of PDEs that says small changes in inputs produce small changes in outputs. This property is the bridge linking 'residual is small' to 'solution is accurate.'

Universal approximation: neural networks can approximate any smooth function arbitrarily well, and with the right structure, they can approximate derivatives too. This ensures solutions exist in theory.

Quadrature approximation: since you can't integrate over the whole domain by hand, you sample at points and average—as you add points, this approximation converges to the true integral, so training loss becomes reliable.
Well-posedness: the PINN problem is mathematically legitimate; there exists at least one neural network that makes the residual small. Whether you find it via optimization is a different question.
The chain of implications: good network → small residual → small training loss (with enough points) → small true error (if coercivity holds).
Failure modes: PINNs break if you can't train the network well, if you don't have enough quadrature points, if the PDE lacks stability, or if stability constants are huge.
AaChPylEH6U.worked_intuition: Take the one-dimensional heat equation: how temperature changes over time equals how much it spreads in space. The true solution is some temperature field u(x,t) that satisfies this. A PINN guesses a solution using a neural network u_net(x,t). To check the guess, it computes: (∂u_net/∂t) − (∂²u_net/∂x²) at several random points in space-time. Call this residual r. When r is near zero, the network's guess obeys the heat equation. The network learns by reducing |r| at those sample points. Now, because the heat equation is stable (small perturbations to the forcing term cause small changes in temperature), if r stays small everywhere, then u_net must be close to the true solution u. The training loss is just the average of |r|² at sample points. Make the training loss tiny, add more sample points so the average converges to the true integral, and the network's error shrinks. That's the whole mechanism.
AaChPylEH6U.where_it_breaks: This approach fails in several ways. First, if you can't train the network well—if gradient descent gets stuck in a bad local minimum—the training loss stays large, so the residual stays large, so the solution is wrong. Second, if you don't have enough quadrature points, the training loss becomes a poor proxy for the true residual; you might think the residual is small when it's actually not. Third, if the PDE itself lacks coercivity—if small input perturbations can produce huge solution changes—then even a small residual doesn't guarantee a small error. Fourth, for nonlinear PDEs, the coercivity constant can depend on the solution itself in complicated ways, making it hard to predict when training will succeed. Finally, in high dimensions, the curse of dimensionality can make sampling impractical: you might need exponentially many quadrature points to cover the domain well.
AaChPylEH6U.takeaway: Physics-informed neural networks work because the PDE equation itself acts as a teacher: by making the network's output approximately satisfy the equation (small residual), and by using mathematical stability properties of well-posed PDEs, you indirectly force the output to approximate the true solution—without ever needing ground-truth examples. This beautiful idea rests on universality of neural networks and stability of PDEs, but it's fragile: it fails whenever training is hard, sampling is sparse, or the PDE is inherently unstable.

BYKaaXPVlDc.plain_title: Why Physics-Informed Neural Networks Work: Connecting Training Error to Real Solutions
BYKaaXPVlDc.big_question: When we train a neural network to satisfy a physics equation (a PDE) instead of matching data, how do we know the network is actually solving the equation correctly? What hidden mechanisms ensure that minimizing training error leads to the true solution?
BYKaaXPVlDc.everyday_anchor: Imagine you're fitting a curve through invisible data by checking whether the curve obeys a known physical law (like the heat equation) at sampled points. You can't see the true answer, only whether your curve follows the rules. How much must you follow the rules before you're actually right?
walkthrough: The core problem is simple but deep: in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), we don't have access to the true solution of a PDE. Instead, we train by forcing the neural network to satisfy the PDE itself at randomly chosen points in space-time. We measure how well it satisfies the equation—this is called the residual—and minimize that. But the residual is an integral over the whole domain, which we can't actually compute. In practice, we approximate it using a sum over a finite number of sample points (a technique from numerical analysis called quadrature). The leap of faith is that if we get the residual small enough via training, and if we sample enough points, then the network will actually be close to the true solution.

To understand this, the lecturer breaks it into three connected questions, working backwards from what we want. Question 1: If the residual is small (meaning the network nearly satisfies the PDE), does that guarantee the total error—the difference between the network and the true solution—is also small? The answer depends entirely on properties of the PDE itself, not the network. The key property is called coercivity, which is a mathematician's way of saying the PDE is stable: small changes in the inputs lead to proportionally small changes in the solution. Formally, if two different right-hand sides differ by a tiny amount, their solutions differ by at most a constant times that amount.

Here's the crucial insight for coercivity: take the original PDE (D times u equals f, where D is some differential operator) and imagine a slightly perturbed version where u-bar satisfies the same equation but with a different right-hand side. The coercivity property says that the difference between u and u-bar in some norm is bounded by a constant times the difference in the right-hand sides. Now plug in your neural network approximation as u-bar. By the coercivity bound, the error is proportional to how much the network fails to satisfy the PDE—exactly the residual. Therefore, if coercivity holds and the residual is small, the total error must be small too. This transforms an intractable problem (directly matching the true solution, which we don't know) into a tractable one (making the PDE residual small).

But there's a catch: coercivity is not automatic. The lecturer gives the heat equation as an example of a PDE that is coercive—the constant doesn't blow up—so pins work well there. Nonlinear equations like Navier-Stokes are trickier. For Navier-Stokes, the constant in the coercivity bound depends on the solution's vorticity (how much the fluid is spinning). If the vorticity explodes, the constant blows up and the bound becomes useless: a small residual no longer guarantees small error. This is the first failure mode: coercivity can fail or become so pessimistic that it ceases to be useful.

Moving to Question 2: Does small training error guarantee small residual? Here's where quadrature approximation matters. The true residual is an integral, but we compute it as a sum over n sample points. Classical numerical analysis tells us that the error in this approximation shrinks as n grows larger. With Monte Carlo sampling, the error goes down like 1/√n. With smoother functions and better quadrature rules, it can decay much faster. So if you make the training error (the sum) small enough and take enough sample points, the true residual (the integral) will be close to the training error and hence also small. Again, the constant here depends on how smooth the residual function is, but for smooth PDEs this is usually reasonable.

Question 3—can we actually make the training error small in practice?—is the hardest. Neural networks are universal approximators in theory, meaning they can represent any continuous function given enough parameters. But in practice, training is nonconvex and getting stuck in bad local minima is a real problem. The lecturer shows numerical experiments on the heat equation where they can indeed achieve small training error, and moreover, the total error tracks the training error beautifully. For every test case shown (heat, Black-Scholes option pricing, Navier-Stokes with low vorticity), small training error led to small total error in practice. However, this isn't guaranteed—it works when the architecture and initialization align with the problem's structure.

The deeper story is that PINNs succeed when two things align: the PDE itself has the right mathematical structure (coercivity with reasonable constants), and the optimization landscape allows the network to find a solution. When the PDE is linear (like the heat equation or Black-Scholes), coercivity is automatic and the constant is explicitly related to the inverse of the differential operator. When the PDE is nonlinear (like full Navier-Stokes), coercivity can still hold, but the constant depends on features of the solution (its norm, its vorticity, its regularity). If those features blow up, PINNs fail. The examples in the lecture show cases where the vorticity stays bounded and everything works, but the lecturer hints that there are regimes where high vorticity or other nonlinear phenomena can derail training.

Putting it together: minimize training error → residual stays small (quadrature approximation, requires many sample points and smooth functions) → total error stays small (coercivity, requires PDE to be stable and its constants to be reasonable). This three-step chain is the complete mechanism. It's neither magic nor automatic. It depends on the specific PDE, the choice of sample points, the network architecture, and the quality of optimization. The lecture provides computable bounds showing these relationships rigorously, validates them numerically, and identifies where they break down.
key_ideas: Residual-based learning: Instead of comparing to unknown true solutions, minimize how much the network violates the PDE equation itself (the residual). This flips the problem from impossible to solvable.
