Why are neural networks so useful? Because of the universal approximation theorem. This says: with enough parameters (weights and biases), a neural network can approximate any continuous function to arbitrary accuracy. Unlike polynomial regression (which is limited to polynomial shapes) or linear regression (which is limited to lines), a neural network is flexible enough to learn almost any mapping from input to output. This is why they work for image classification, time series prediction, and even learning physics equations.

Now, how do we actually find those weights? For polynomial regression, there is an analytical formula using linear algebra. For neural networks, there is no formula, so we use gradient descent. We compute how much the loss (the squared error between prediction and ground truth) changes when we slightly adjust each weight. The direction of steepest descent tells us which way to tweak the weights to reduce the loss. We take many small steps in that direction, and gradually the network learns to fit the data. This is where backpropagation comes in: it is just an efficient algorithm for computing these gradients using the chain rule. You do a forward pass (compute the output), store the intermediate layer outputs, then do a backward pass where you propagate the gradient signal from the loss back through all the layers to compute the gradient with respect to every weight.

Different problems call for different network architectures. For images, a convolutional neural network (CNN) is much smarter than a fully-connected network. Instead of every neuron connecting to every input pixel (which would require millions of weights), each neuron in a CNN looks at only a small patch of the image. All neurons apply the same filter (share weights), so a 3×3 filter applied to an image only needs 9 weights, not millions. This dramatically reduces the number of parameters, making the network more efficient and less prone to overfitting. CNNs also have translational equivariance: if you slide a dog's head to a different part of the image, the CNN learns the same features.

The real power of deep learning comes from depth. A shallow network might need exponentially more neurons to match the performance of a deep network. Research showed that for image classification, the depth (number of layers) matters much more than width (number of neurons per layer). Early layers detect simple edges and corners; middle layers find nose-like and ear-like shapes; deep layers recognize entire faces. This hierarchical feature learning emerges naturally from training the network end-to-end. We encode this compositional structure as an inductive bias in the architecture itself, and it works.

Finally, there are different ways to use neural networks depending on your problem. Supervised learning: you have input-output pairs and you want to predict outputs from inputs (regression if outputs are continuous, classification if they are discrete categories). Unsupervised learning: you only have inputs, and you want the network to discover patterns or compress the data (autoencoders) or generate new samples that look like the training data (generative models). Autoregressive models: you have sequences and you want to predict the next value given the history (how language models like ChatGPT work). In all cases, the core idea remains: the neural network is a flexible function, and we are fitting it to data by adjusting its weights to minimize a loss.
key_ideas: A neural network is a flexible mathematical function (like a curve) that we fit to data by adjusting its weights and biases to minimize prediction error.
Activation functions (like ReLU or tanh) introduce nonlinearity, allowing networks to bend and fit complicated patterns instead of collapsing into straight lines.
Universal approximation: with enough layers and neurons, a neural network can learn to approximate any continuous function, which is why they are so general-purpose.
Backpropagation is an efficient algorithm that uses the chain rule to compute how much each weight contributed to the overall error, enabling gradient descent training.
Architecture matters: convolutional networks for images reduce parameters by having neurons look at only small patches and share weights; depth matters more than width.
Different tasks (supervised, unsupervised, autoregressive) all use the same underlying principle: fit a flexible function to data using loss functions and gradient-based optimization.
OXmLwCQA7F4.worked_intuition: Imagine training a network to fit a wavy curve. Start with a random flat function. Backpropagation measures: 'your current prediction at point x=2 is too high by 0.5, and if we increase weight w1 by 0.01 it would improve by 0.03.' The algorithm discovers the gradient—the direction of steepest descent. We take a small step in that direction. After many steps, the function curves and bends to match the data. The key insight: we never analytically solve for weights. Instead, we iteratively measure error, compute gradients, and adjust. This is why autod tools like PyTorch are essential—they automate gradient computation so we only define what the forward function does, and the approach computes the backward gradient pass automatically.
OXmLwCQA7F4.where_it_breaks: Neural networks require a lot of training data to work well. With tiny datasets, a simple polynomial fit may work better because neural networks have so many parameters they can overfit (memorize noise instead of learning true patterns). Computational cost scales with network size; training huge models requires effective hardware (GPUs, TPUs) and careful engineering. Neural networks are also notoriously hard to interpret—because the representation is distributed across many neurons, it is difficult to understand which weights are responsible for which predictions. Finally, universal approximation is a theoretical guarantee (given enough parameters), but it does not tell you how many parameters you need or whether gradient descent will actually find the global minimum in practice.
OXmLwCQA7F4.takeaway: Neural networks are not magical: they are flexible functions that we fit to data using gradient descent and backpropagation, just like polynomial regression, but more effective because they can compose many nonlinear layers. The art of deep learning is choosing the right architecture (fully-connected, convolutional, recurrent, etc.) for your problem and letting backprop do the work of learning the weights.

S11QK8baGVI.plain_title: Why Physics-Informed Neural Networks Are Slow, and How to Fix Them
S11QK8baGVI.big_question: Physics-informed neural networks promise to solve differential equations using machine learning—but they're often much slower than traditional numerical methods. What are the real bottlenecks, and what practical techniques actually make them competitive?
S11QK8baGVI.everyday_anchor: Imagine you're predicting earthquake waves through the earth. A traditional simulator takes one minute. A neural network trying the same thing takes an hour—and then has to retrain from scratch when you move the earthquake to a different location. Why is it so slow, and what can you do about it?
walkthrough: Physics-informed neural networks (PINs) solve differential equations by training a neural network to satisfy both boundary conditions and the physics equation itself. Instead of computing solutions on a fixed grid like traditional methods do, PINs give you a smooth function you can evaluate anywhere. This sounds great, but there's a hidden cost: you have to compute the network's gradients (how its output changes with respect to position and time) millions of times during training, and that takes an enormous amount of computation on a GPU. A seemingly simple 2D wave problem that takes 60 seconds on a traditional method can take an hour on a neural network, making it completely uncompetitive.

The real killer is reusability. In traditional simulation, once you solve for one earthquake location, you can instantly solve for a nearby earthquake—the program just runs again quickly. With PINs, the network was trained for a specific earthquake source location, so if you move the source even slightly, you have to retrain the entire network from scratch. This means for practical problems where you need many scenarios, you're paying the one-hour cost repeatedly. It's not just slow; it's wasteful.

The first major fix is conditioning: instead of training one network per scenario, train a single network that takes the source location (or other parameters) as an extra input alongside the spatial coordinates. During training, you sample over many source locations, boundary conditions, and initial configurations. Once trained, this network can instantly predict the solution for any combination of parameters without retraining. You're no longer throwing away computation; you're building a reusable surrogate model that answers 'what if' questions at the speed of a forward network pass.

A second approach is discretization: instead of having the network output a continuous function, have it output solution values on a fixed grid (like a matrix of pressure values). You replace exact gradients (which are expensive to compute) with finite differences (which are cheap—just arithmetic on neighboring grid points). This feels like stepping backward toward traditional methods, but it's not—you're still using a learnable neural network architecture, just with approximate gradients instead of exact ones. The trade-off is speed: you get 2-4x speedup by using finite differences instead of automatic differentiation.

Here's the mathematical payoff: with discretized PINs, you can use fancy architectures like convolutional networks that exploit grid structure. You add hard boundary constraints by padding the output grid with known values, so the boundary loss term vanishes entirely—no more tuning the tricky Lambda weights that balance boundary versus physics terms. A landmark 2021 paper showed this approach needs no simulation data to train; it only needs the physics equation itself plus the input domain description. Yet it generalizes better than pure data-driven methods when tested on scenarios outside the training distribution, suggesting the physics constraint teaches the network something reliable about the underlying system.

The third speed-up is to replace expensive automatic differentiation with finite difference approximations. By taking differences of the network output at nearby points instead of backpropagating gradients, you reduce training time by another factor of 2-4. The downside is approximation error: you lose the exact gradients, and tuning the 'step size' of your finite difference window becomes important. But for many problems, the speed gain is worth it.

All these fixes address the same root problem: automatic differentiation is computationally expensive at scale. PINs work by imposing the physics equation as a soft constraint during training, which requires computing gradients, which requires autodiff. Each fix sidesteps or cheapens that bottleneck. Conditioning lets one network serve many problems. Discretization lets you use cheap finite differences instead of autodiff. The key insight is that PINs don't need to be 'pure' to be useful—they work even if you approximate the gradients or restrict them to a grid.

But every fix introduces a trade-off. Conditioned networks lose the mesh-free property—they work best for fixed geometries. Discretized PINs depend on a fixed mesh, so you can't query the solution at arbitrary points like you could with the original formulation. Finite differences are approximate, so they accumulate error. There is no universal 'fast PIN' that beats every alternative in every scenario. The practical choice depends on your problem: Is speed or generalization more important? Do you have a fixed geometry? How many scenarios do you need to solve? The extensions give you tools to answer these questions, but you have to pick the right tool.
key_ideas: Automatic differentiation is the bottleneck—computing exact gradients during training makes standard PINs slow because the network's output derivatives must be computed thousands of times
Conditioning a PIN on extra inputs (like source location or initial conditions) lets a single trained network serve many scenarios, replacing retraining with fast inference
Discretized PINs output solution values on a fixed grid and use finite differences for gradients instead of autodiff, achieving 2-4x speedup at the cost of losing the mesh-free property
Physics constraints can teach networks reliability even without simulation data; unsupervised discretized PINs outgeneralize purely data-driven methods on out-of-distribution inputs
Every computational speed-up introduces a trade-off: conditioning sacrifices mesh-freedom, discretization fixes the geometry, finite differences trade exact gradients for approximation error
S11QK8baGVI.worked_intuition: Picture training a standard PIN to predict seismic waves from an earthquake. The network takes (x, y, z, t) coordinates as input and outputs pressure. To satisfy the wave equation, you need dP/dt and dP/dx and dP/dz—gradients of the output. Computing these via automatic differentiation for thousands of training points is slow. Now imagine instead conditioning the network: add the earthquake source location (xs, ys) as extra inputs. Train on earthquakes scattered across a region. Once done, you query the network with any source location—no retraining. Speed comes from amortizing the training cost across many scenarios. Alternatively, discretize: instead of a continuous function, the network outputs a 3D pressure grid (say, 100×100×100 values). To compute gradients, just subtract neighboring grid values (finite difference)—arithmetic, not autodiff. You lose the ability to query at arbitrary points, but you gain speed and can use convolutional layers. Both strategies work; neither dominates everything.
S11QK8baGVI.where_it_breaks: Conditioned PINs work best when the parameter space is bounded (earthquake locations within a region, not anywhere on Earth) and the domain geometry is fixed. Discretized PINs are locked to their training grid resolution and geometry—you can't simulate at higher resolution without retraining. Finite difference approximations accumulate error and require tuning the step size. None of these fixes make PINs faster than traditional methods for simple, forward-only simulations on regular geometries; traditional methods still win there. PINs shine when you need inverse problems (finding parameters from data), when the geometry is irregular, or when you want to solve many coupled problems simultaneously. The extensions fix computational speed but don't address the underlying issue that standard neural networks struggle with high-frequency oscillations—a deeper limitation requiring architectural innovation (which the next lecture covers).
S11QK8baGVI.takeaway: Slow PINs aren't fundamentally broken; they're solving a harder problem than traditional simulators (learning from physics instead of numerical discretization). The practical extensions—conditioning for parameter reuse, discretization for cheap gradients, finite differences for speed—are not Band-Aids. They're recognizing that PINs don't need to be pure to be useful. Pick the variant that matches your problem: Do you need one solution or many? Fixed geometry or arbitrary domains? Speed or exactness? The extensions give you a toolkit; the right choice depends on your constraints.

T89vWHjqis8.plain_title: Why We Need AI to Solve the Laws of Nature: The Problem with Classical Methods
T89vWHjqis8.big_question: Scientists and engineers understand the laws governing everything from heat diffusion to aircraft flight through mathematical equations. But once you write the equations down, how do you actually solve them? And why does it become impossibly slow as problems get bigger or more intricate?
T89vWHjqis8.everyday_anchor: Imagine you want to design a faster airplane wing. You know the physics: the Navier-Stokes equations describe how air flows. A computer can solve these equations, but on a realistic 3D aircraft, it takes 500 hours of supercomputer time for just one simulation. If you need thousands of designs to optimize the shape, you are stuck. The calculation is correct but computationally impossible.
walkthrough: For 300 years, scientists have described natural phenomena using differential equations—starting with Newton. These are mathematical statements that say how things change over space and time. A tsunami? Modeled by fluid equations. A cloud formation? Conservation of mass, momentum, and energy. A cancer tumor spreading? Diffusion equations. Quantum mechanics, chemical reactions, financial options—all follow this pattern. The unifying principle is simple: write down the differential equations that capture the physical laws, then solve them.

But here is the catch: most of these equations are impossible to solve by hand. You cannot write down a formula for the answer. Even simple-looking equations like the heat equation (which Fourier derived to cool hot cannon barrels) require clever approximations. So since the 1920s, scientists have used numerical methods: finite differences, finite elements, spectral methods. These divide space and time into a grid of points, replace calculus derivatives with simple arithmetic, and let computers iterate step by step. This works beautifully—it is how we simulate weather, design planes, and understand the sun.

The fatal weakness emerges when you scale up. To get 1% accuracy (the engineering standard), the computational cost grows exponentially with dimensionality. In 1D (one direction), it might take 1,000 units of compute. In 2D (a flat surface), 10,000. In 3D (the real world), 100,000. Jump to 100 dimensions (common in finance or quantum systems), and the method collapses entirely. The cost is proportional to roughly 10^(dimension+2), which is insurmountable for realistic problems.

Even in three dimensions, the wall is immediate and practical. A high-resolution simulation of the Navier-Stokes equations (the physics of fluid flow around a car or aircraft) needs billions of grid points. Each time step takes minutes. Simulating it all the way to a steady state takes hours or days on a supercomputer. Now add the design problem: you want to tweak the shape to reduce drag. Each tiny design change requires a full re-simulation. An aircraft company needs thousands of simulations to find a good design. At 500 hours per simulation, it becomes years of computation. No designer can wait that long. They settle for conservative, sub-optimal designs because exploring the space is impossible.

A second, subtler problem emerges: the classical workflow assumes you know the equations. But in many real systems—biology, geology, medicine—you do not fully know the governing laws. You have data: observations, measurements, time series. But you must guess at the equations that explain them, then solve those guesses. If the guess is wrong, the simulations are wrong. And even if your equations are right, they might be so stiff (some parts change much faster than others) or so chaotic (tiny changes in initial conditions cascade into wildly different outcomes) that numerical methods become unreliable. You cannot confidently optimize a design or make a prediction when the uncertainty is baked into the method itself.

This is the gap the course addresses: instead of the slow, expensive cycle of write-equations → solve-numerically → iterate, what if you could learn a fast surrogate? A surrogate is a neural network or other learned function that acts like the equations but evaluates in milliseconds instead of hours. Train it once on a handful of expensive simulations, then use it to evaluate thousands of designs instantly. Or, if you do not know the exact equations, let the network infer them from data. This is the core of physics-informed machine learning: marry the physics you do know (or can measure) with the learning power of deep networks to solve the intractable and the uncertain.

But there is a catch to that too: a naive neural network trained only on data will interpolate between the simulations you fed it. Outside that range, it fails. A physics-informed network bakes physical laws (conservation of mass, energy, momentum) directly into the network architecture or loss function, so it respects the physics even where there is no training data. It becomes a learned equation-solver that is fast, accurate, and generalizable—if you build it right. The rest of this course is learning how to do exactly that.

The key insight is this: the classical world divides into domains. Physics and engineering live in the world of equations and numerical solvers. Machine learning lives in the world of data and learned patterns. For 300 years, scientists solved by hand and machine at the expense of time. For the last 20 years, they have tried pure learning, ignoring physics, and gotten brittle systems. The frontier—and the whole point of this course—is combining them: physics-informed learning, where symmetries, conservation laws, and differential equations guide the network, and data helps it learn the details and uncertainties the equations miss.
key_ideas: Differential equations (math statements of how things change) are the universal language of science and engineering—everything from stars to proteins follows them.

Numerical methods approximate the answer by replacing continuous space-time with a discrete grid and doing arithmetic instead of calculus—fast for simple 1D problems, impossibly slow in high dimensions.
The curse of dimensionality: as dimension grows, the cost to achieve fixed accuracy explodes exponentially; 3D fluid simulations take days, 100-dimensional finance problems become untractable.

Design and optimization amplify the cost: one simulation per shape × thousands of candidate shapes means years of supercomputer time, forcing engineers to be conservative and use heuristics instead of rigorous exploration.

Physics-informed machine learning: train a neural network on a small set of expensive simulations and let it learn to predict the outcome (or the dynamics) in milliseconds; embed the physics rules directly into the network so it respects them even outside the training region.

The frontier combines two worlds: the rigor and interpretability of physics-based equations with the flexibility and data-driven learning of neural networks, to solve problems that are too expensive classically and too uncertain for pure learning alone.
T89vWHjqis8.worked_intuition: Take the simplest case: the heat equation in one dimension (a metal rod, cold at the ends, with initial temperature distribution). Classically, you divide the rod into (say) 100 points, divide time into small steps, and update each point in parallel based on its neighbors. Forward 1,000 time steps takes a second on a laptop. Now, a neural network trained on 100 of these simulations (varied initial conditions) learns the operator: it takes the initial temperature distribution and predicts the temperature at any later time, in milliseconds. You can now cheaply answer "what if" questions: if I change the initial profile, what happens? If I want to find an initial condition that reaches a target state, optimization is now tractable. The network is fast because it amortizes the learning across many problems. But it also needs the physics baked in (e.g., temperature cannot violate maximum principles, no energy appears from nowhere) so it does not invent unphysical solutions when it extrapolates to untested regions.
T89vWHjqis8.where_it_breaks: Pure numerical methods fail on high-dimensional problems (100+ dimensions) where the grid becomes impossibly large; they also struggle with chaotic or stiff systems where tiny input changes cause huge output swings or where fast/slow timescales coexist. Pure neural networks trained only on data often fail when you extrapolate beyond the range they saw: they are brittle and unphysical outside the training envelope. Physics-informed networks are much better but still limited if the physics you bake in is incomplete or wrong, or if the data is sparse or noisy in critical regions. The method also assumes you can generate or afford sufficient training data; if a single simulation costs weeks, amassing 1,000 training samples may be impractical. Finally, even with fast surrogates, some inverse problems (inferring internal structure from boundary measurements) and uncertainty quantification (propagating noise and unknowns through a design space) remain genuinely hard and require careful probabilistic modeling.
T89vWHjqis8.takeaway: The whole pipeline of science and engineering—observe nature, write equations, solve them, optimize designs—works brilliantly but breaks under scale and difficulty. Machine learning can patch this by learning fast surrogates from expensive simulations, but only if we teach the network the physics it must obey. This course is about how to do that: building neural networks that respect the laws of conservation and symmetry, that solve PDEs faster than classical methods, that infer missing physics from data, and that scale to real engineering design and discovery.

Tohlijxz3XQ.plain_title: How to Turn Noise Into Pictures: The Backward Diffusion Model
Tohlijxz3XQ.big_question: If we can make pictures disappear into random noise by adding noise step-by-step, can we run that process backward to turn pure noise into real pictures?
Tohlijxz3XQ.everyday_anchor: Imagine a photograph slowly fading into pure static, pixel by pixel, as you add random noise. A diffusion model learns to reverse that—starting from complete TV static, it gradually removes the noise to reconstruct a sharp photo.
walkthrough: Diffusion is a natural process where particles spread out randomly. Think of gas molecules in a sealed room: if you break the seal, they wander randomly outward and mix with the air outside. The same idea works for images: if you treat each pixel as a particle and make it do a random walk (by adding random noise each time step), eventually every image becomes pure random static. This forward process is easy—just add noise. The hard part is learning to run it backward.

Mathematically, we describe this with a stochastic differential equation—a rule for how things change when randomness is involved. The forward process says: each tiny change in the image is made up of two things. First, a deterministic drift (a predictable push in some direction). Second, random noise (the Wiener process, which is a fancy way of saying 'Gaussian noise at each step'). The amount of noise we add is controlled by a diffusion coefficient. Start with a real image, apply this forward SDE long enough, and you end up at pure Gaussian noise.

Here's the remarkable part: there exists a reverse SDE. In the 1980s, Anderson proved that if you know the probability distribution of images at every time step, you can write down an SDE that runs backward in time. Start from pure noise and solve this backward SDE, and you arrive at a sample from your original data distribution—a real image. The catch: this backward SDE depends on something we don't know—the probability distribution of images at each time step. But we can train a neural network to learn it.

Instead of learning the full distribution, we train a network to learn the score function: the gradient of the logarithm of the probability. Think of probability as a landscape; the score points uphill. At any noisy image and any time step, the score tells you which direction to move to find images that are 'more probable.' We parameterize this with a neural network that takes two inputs (the noisy image and the time step) and outputs a vector the same shape as the image—the direction to move.

To train this network, we use a loss function derived from the forward process. Here's the key insight: when you apply the forward SDE to a clean image, the noisy image at time t is just the original image plus some Gaussian noise. The amount of noise depends on t. We can compute the true score analytically for this case. So the loss function says: the network should predict the score, which turns out to be equivalent to predicting the noise that was added. During training, we sample random clean images, random time steps, add the corresponding noise, and teach the network to predict that noise. This is simpler and more stable than trying to match distributions directly.

Once trained, generating images is straightforward. Start with pure random noise (sample from a Gaussian). Solve the learned backward SDE from time T to time 0, using your trained neural network as the score function. At each step, the network tells you how to steer the noise toward higher probability. You can use any numerical solver—Euler's method works fine. There's even a deterministic version: an ordinary differential equation (ODE) that produces a single path without randomness but still samples from your learned distribution.

To use diffusion models for inverse problems—like reconstructing a CT image from a sinogram (the scanner measurement)—we interleave two forces. As we reverse the diffusion (denoising), at each time step we also add a small optimization step: we compute the gradient of the measurement loss (how well the current image matches the observed data) and nudge the image toward satisfying that constraint. This hybrid approach marries two ideas: the diffusion model enforces that the result looks like a real CT image, and the optimization enforces that it matches the actual measurement. The result is an image that is both physically realistic and consistent with the observations.

The power of this method is generality. Whether your forward process is adding noise to images, modeling stock price evolution, or describing other physical processes, the same math applies. You learn a score function, reverse the process, and sample from your learned distribution. For inverse problems in science, diffusion models offer a principled way to blend physical constraints with data priors, avoiding overfitting and producing physically plausible solutions. The link to neural differential equations runs deep: the trained model is itself a learnable differential equation that produces realistic samples.
key_ideas: Forward diffusion is simple: repeatedly add noise until an image becomes pure static. It's the reverse we need to learn.
The score function is the gradient of log-probability—it points in the direction of 'more likely' images. A neural network learns to approximate it.
Training the score network reduces to predicting the noise added at each step, which is tractable and stable.
Once trained, generate images by starting from noise and iteratively denoising using the learned score, guided by a differential equation solver.
For science: interleave denoising with optimization to satisfy measurement constraints, creating images that are both realistic and consistent with observations.
Diffusion models are interpretable as neural differential equations, providing a bridge between deep learning and classical scientific computing.
Tohlijxz3XQ.worked_intuition: Let's trace one example. You have a 64×64 image of a handwritten digit. In the forward process, you add Gaussian noise (scaled by the time step) repeatedly: the image becomes increasingly blurry and grainy until, after T steps, it's indistinguishable from random pixels. To reverse it, your trained score network receives both the noisy image at each step t and the time value. It outputs a 64×64 image (the same shape) predicting the noise. In practice, this is learned as: network predicts noise minus original image divided by noise standard deviation at time t. As you solve the backward equation from t=T down to t=0, at each step the network nudges the image to align with the learned probability of true digits. You never 'condition' on a label—the reverse SDE only depends on the noisy image and time. Yet if your training data was balanced across all digits, the final image will look like one of them, randomly chosen.
Tohlijxz3XQ.where_it_breaks: The method assumes the backward SDE is well-defined, which requires knowing the score function everywhere. In practice, you train only on the times and images your forward process samples; you never see true images that are extremely noisy, so the network's predictions there may be unreliable. Solving the backward ODE in many steps is slow—you're running a neural network hundreds of times per image. For high-resolution images (megapixels), memory and compute explode. For inverse problems, the method works best when the forward operator (the scanner model) is fast to compute gradients through; if it's truly opaque model, the proximal optimization step won't work. Finally, the quality of generated images depends entirely on the quality and diversity of training data; poor or biased data produces poor or biased samples.
Tohlijxz3XQ.takeaway: Diffusion models reverse a natural process by learning to predict noise at every stage, then run that prediction backward. For science, they blend a learned prior (images that look realistic) with measurement constraints (equations that respect observations), producing solutions that are both physically plausible and data-consistent.

UiZxDRBd0Q8.plain_title: Why Partial Differential Equations are the Language of Physical Science—and What Breaks When We Try to Solve Them
UiZxDRBd0Q8.big_question: From atoms to galaxies, how do we describe what happens in nature? And why is predicting even simple systems so impossibly expensive on a computer?
UiZxDRBd0Q8.everyday_anchor: Think of heat spreading through a room. Right now, temperature is different in different places and changing over time. There's no simple formula to tell you the temperature at any point and moment—but there is a rule (an equation) that governs how heat flows.
walkthrough: Start with a basic observation: the world works by rules. When you heat one side of a room, warmth spreads. When a star explodes, gravitational waves ripple outward. When a drug dissolves in water, concentration changes. All these phenomena follow laws—physical laws. Herbert Simon, a Nobel laureate who studied intricate systems, pointed out that science works by a simple method: given a description of a natural phenomenon, find the differential equations that govern it. A differential equation is a mathematical relationship that connects a quantity (like temperature) to how it changes—either over time or across space. A partial differential equation, or PDE, handles quantities that change in multiple ways at once: in time, and in different directions of space.

Here is the key insight: almost every physical system in nature is described by a PDE. Take something as simple as temperature in a room. At any point in space, at any moment in time, there is a temperature. The room is three-dimensional, so temperature varies as you move left or right, forward or backward, up or down. It also varies as time passes—warmer during the day, cooler at night. The physical law (Fourier's law, named after the mathematician Joseph Fourier) says that heat flows from hot to cold, and the rate of flow depends on how steep the temperature gradient is—how quickly temperature changes as you move through space. When you write down this law mathematically, you get a PDE relating the temperature and its spatial and temporal derivatives (rates of change). The same pattern appears everywhere: the Schrödinger equation, which describes electrons in atoms, is a PDE. The Einstein field equations of general relativity are PDEs. The Navier-Stokes equations, which govern fluid flow in the atmosphere, oceans, and aircraft wings, are PDEs. Reaction-diffusion equations describe how patterns form on animal wings. The scale ranges from subatomic particles to the entire universe—30 to 50 orders of magnitude in size—yet all are described by PDEs. This is the beauty and power of mathematics: one language captures vastly different phenomena.

Now comes the hard part: we cannot solve most of these equations by hand. There is no pen-and-paper formula. Even Einstein himself, who wrote down his equations in 1915, could only solve them in very special cases. For 175 years, from roughly 1757 (when Euler wrote his fluid equations) until the late 1920s, scientists tried to solve PDEs by finding clever tricks—Taylor expansions, asymptotic approximations, matching coefficients. Then everything changed. A physicist named Lewis Richardson realized that you could use a computer (even the analog computers of that era) to approximate solutions numerically. The idea is simple: instead of solving the equation everywhere and at every time, you pick a grid of discrete points in space and time. At each point, you approximate the derivatives (rates of change) using finite differences—simple arithmetic operations. You replace the continuous problem with a discrete one. For example, in a one-dimensional domain, instead of asking 'what is the temperature everywhere?', you ask 'what is the temperature at these 100 points?' The time derivative becomes a simple ratio: how much the temperature changes from one time step to the next. The spatial derivative becomes another ratio: how much temperature changes from one grid point to the next. You then march through time, using the old values to predict the new values. This method is 100 years old and works extraordinarily well. Modern computers using finite difference, finite element, or spectral methods can simulate supernova core collapse in 3D, cumulus cloud formation, tsunami generation, and airflow around rockets—all successfully tested against reality.

But there is a hidden cost that makes these classical methods break down. To get a small error in your answer, your mesh (grid spacing) has to be small, and your time steps have to be tiny. The time step must scale as the square of the mesh size (a stability requirement called the Courant condition). The error in your answer also scales as the square of the mesh size. This means the computational cost has a brutal scaling law: in one dimension, you need roughly 1/mesh_size mesh points; in two dimensions, you need (1/mesh_size)² points; in three dimensions, (1/mesh_size)³ points. The time cost scales similarly. Putting it together: the total computational cost grows as (1/mesh_size)^(5/2) in three dimensions. If you want a 1% error—that is, error of 1/100—you need 100^(5/2) = 100,000 times more computation. And that is before you account for the constant factors in the scaling law. In higher dimensions, the situation becomes absurd. For a 10-dimensional problem (common in quantum mechanics and some inverse problems), the scaling factor is dimension^6, or 10^6 = 1 million times more compute just for the extra dimensions. For 100 dimensions, it is 100 million times. This is the curse of dimensionality: traditional numerical methods break down in high dimensions.

Real-world costs illustrate the pain. Boeing spends approximately 2 billion dollars per year on computational budgets—much of it for simulating airflow around aircraft wings to optimize wing shape. This is a 'many-query problem': you start with a wing design, simulate the flow to compute lift and drag (solve the Navier-Stokes equations once), then adjust the shape slightly and repeat—hundreds or thousands of iterations. Each PDE solve is expensive; doing it hundreds of times is prohibitively expensive. Similarly, in seismic imaging, you have sensors on the ground detecting echoes from sound waves sent into the earth. From these echoes, you want to infer the geological structure (the speed at which waves travel through rock). This is an inverse problem: you know the wave equation and the sensor outputs, but you must infer the wave speed. The standard approach is iterative: guess a wave speed, solve the forward problem, check if it matches the data, then adjust your guess. This takes 100 to 10,000 iterations of the PDE solver. For uncertainty quantification in turbulent flows, you need statistics (mean, variance) over many independent samples, not just one solution. A high-resolution simulation might cost 100 node-hours on a supercomputer per sample, and if you need 1,000 samples to get stable statistics, that is 100,000 node-hours total—equivalent to roughly half a million Swiss francs if you had to pay out of pocket.

There is another, more subtle problem: missing physics. Yes, the Navier-Stokes equations perfectly describe fluid motion, but in climate modeling, you also need to account for vegetation, land absorption and reflection, ocean circulation, and radiation. The physics of how a forest affects climate, or how soil properties influence local weather, is either approximate or completely unknown. These are empirical relationships without first-principles derivations. Traffic flow in a city can be modeled roughly like fluid flow, but there is no fundamental theory. Flow in the brain involves biological circuits we do not understand. In all these cases, the underlying physics is either expensive to simulate, incompletely known, or both. You have lots of data but incomplete equations. This is the problem the course will address: can we use machine learning not to replace physics entirely, but to augment incomplete physics with data, or to dramatically speed up expensive simulations?

The core challenge distills to three issues. First: computational cost grows exponentially with problem dimension, making high-dimensional and many-query problems infeasible. Second: grid generation is hard for irregular domains, and the method requires re-discretizing if the domain changes. Third: when physics is missing or approximate, traditional numerical methods are useless—you cannot solve an equation you do not fully know. The entire course is built on the premise that we should combine classical physics (the PDEs we do know, because they are reliable) with modern machine learning (to learn the parts we do not know, or to accelerate the expensive parts). The next lecture will introduce physics-informed neural networks, which encode known PDEs directly into a neural network's loss function, so the network learns to be a solution to the PDE while also learning from data.
key_ideas: Partial differential equations (PDEs): equations relating a quantity and how it changes in space and time. They are the universal language of physics—atoms, weather, fluid flow, gravity all speak in PDEs

Discretization: breaking a continuous domain into a grid of discrete points and approximating derivatives using finite differences. This allows computers to solve PDEs, and it has worked for 100 years

Curse of dimensionality: the computational cost of traditional numerical methods scales exponentially with the dimension of the problem. A 10D problem costs roughly 1 million times more than a 1D problem for the same accuracy

Many-query and inverse problems: real applications often require solving the PDE hundreds or thousands of times (e.g., aircraft design, seismic imaging, optimization). Each solve is expensive, making the total cost prohibitive
Missing physics: some systems (climate, traffic, biological flows) are described by incomplete equations, or the equations are known but so expensive to solve that alternatives are needed

Scaling laws: error scales as (mesh_size)², time step must be proportional to (mesh_size)², and total compute cost grows as (1/mesh_size)^(d+1) in d dimensions. This is a hard mathematical fact, not a limitation of implementation

Why machine learning matters: when physics equations are expensive, incomplete, or require many evaluations, machine learning can learn surrogates from data, fill in missing pieces, or accelerate expensive solves
UiZxDRBd0Q8.worked_intuition: Imagine you want to predict how temperature spreads in a one-meter-long rod after you heat one end. You discretize into 100 points. To get a 1% error in your answer, you need roughly 100 mesh points, which is fine. But now imagine a 3D room—a cube 10 meters on a side. If you use 100 points per side, you have 100³ = 1 million grid points total. The time step must be (1/100)² = 0.0001 relative time units. To simulate, say, one hour, you might need 100,000 time steps. Per time step, you do a handful of arithmetic operations per point, so 1 million × 100,000 = 100 billion operations. A modern CPU does ~10 billion operations per second, so this takes ~10 seconds—manageable. But now increase resolution to 1,000 points per side (more realistic for engineering). You have 1 billion grid points and 1 million time steps, or 10^15 operations—10,000 seconds, nearly 3 hours on a single processor. If you want 0.1% error instead of 1%, you need 10 times finer mesh, which is 10^4 times more operations: 100,000 seconds, nearly a day. This is why supercomputers exist, and why a single simulation can cost half a million dollars. Machine learning can learn a function that maps initial conditions directly to final temperature distribution, bypassing the expensive marching-in-time process, if it can learn from data.

WP02-hpKB-4.plain_title: How to learn solution operators for PDEs without breaking resolution independence
WP02-hpKB-4.big_question: When we build neural networks to learn PDE solutions, why do they fail to generalize across different grid resolutions, and how can we design networks that work faithfully at any resolution?
WP02-hpKB-4.everyday_anchor: Imagine you learn to recognize a person's face from a photo at 100×100 pixels. Later, you get a 200×200 pixel version of the same person—are the pixel values at each location identical? No. So your network trained on specific pixel positions sees different inputs, even though it's the same underlying face. PDEs have the same problem: functions are the same, but sampled values differ with resolution.
walkthrough: The core problem starts with two worlds that never quite fit together: infinite-dimensional mathematics and finite-dimensional computers. PDEs live in infinite dimensions—a solution is a continuous function defined everywhere. But we compute on grids, which are finite samples. The key insight from signal processing (going back to Shannon and earlier) is that you can map perfectly between these worlds IF certain conditions hold. Band-limited functions—functions whose frequency content stops at some finite cutoff—can be exactly reconstructed from equally-spaced samples, provided you sample densely enough. Specifically, if the highest frequency in your function is ω, you need at least 2ω+1 grid points. This is the Nyquist barrier. As long as you stay above this barrier, discretization introduces zero error: the sampled values and the continuous function are completely equivalent.

Now let's see why standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) fail. A CNN uses discrete convolutions: you slide a fixed-size kernel window over discrete grid points and compute outputs. This is perfectly fine if you always work with the exact same grid. But when you change the grid resolution, everything breaks. Here's the invisible failure: your kernel hits three specific grid points during training (say, at positions 0.0, 0.25, 0.5). During testing on a finer grid, it hits three new points at positions (0.0, 0.125, 0.25). Even though these functions are band-limited and represent the same underlying solution, the specific pixel values are different. The kernel doesn't 'know' it's seeing the same function—it only sees different numbers. These small differences compound through layers, and errors grow explosively. The network cannot generalize because the convolution operation is tied to the discrete grid itself, not the underlying continuous function.

Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) tried a different approach: instead of convolving in physical space, apply Fourier transforms to switch to frequency space, do the convolution there, then transform back. At first glance this looks better. But FNOs reveal a hidden problem with pointwise nonlinearities. When you apply a nonlinearity like ReLU or squaring to a band-limited function, you create new frequencies that shouldn't exist. Mathematically, if you square a function with frequency components up to 10, you suddenly get components up to frequency 20. This happens because nonlinearities mix modes together—a property of how sine and cosine functions multiply. In FNOs, the Fourier coefficients are truncated to a fixed number of modes, but the nonlinearity breaks the band-limited assumption. After each activation, the output has higher frequency content, which gets aliased and corrupted when you truncate back down. The convolution tries to correct for this in the next layer, but it's fighting a losing battle. You get small errors that accumulate across layers.

To understand how to fix this, we need to think about what it really means to respect the mathematics. The approach of Representation Equivalent Neural Operators (ReNOs) formalizes the idea: learning and discretization should commute. Whether you first project to finite dimensions then learn, or learn then discretize, you should get the same result. This is only possible if the encoding (sampling) and reconstruction (interpolation) operations preserve the structure perfectly. For band-limited functions, sync interpolation does this: given sampled values on a grid, you can exactly reconstruct the continuous function using a special sinc basis, then resample it at any new grid resolution and get back the same values. The miracle of this is that it's not magic—it follows directly from Shannon sampling theory.

Convolutional operators implement this insight in physical space rather than Fourier space. The key move is subtle but elegant: use continuous convolutions on band-limited functions with a discrete kernel. This means your kernel is defined only at discrete points (say, three points), but your input and output are treated as continuous functions. When you want to apply the operator to data on a different grid, you don't apply the kernel directly to the new grid points. Instead, you first use sync interpolation to reconstruct the continuous function from the test-grid samples, then project it back down to your training resolution, apply the kernel there, and you get an answer that is mathematically guaranteed to be identical. This is the trick: you resize the input and output, not the kernel. The Nyquist condition ensures that the interpolation and downsampling lose no information, so you're really operating on the same underlying function.

The nonlinearity problem requires a completely different solution. You cannot apply a pointwise nonlinearity and remain representation-equivalent, because pointwise operations introduce frequencies in an uncontrolled way. Instead, use upsampling-then-nonlinearity-then-downsampling. The idea is to deliberately expand the bandwidth before applying the nonlinearity, creating space for the higher frequencies that will be generated. If your function has 10 frequency components, you artificially expand the representation to allow 20 components (padding the extra ones with zeros), then apply the nonlinearity on this expanded grid where there are enough sample points. After the nonlinearity generates its higher frequencies, you downsample back to your original 10-component space using sync-based filtering. This kills the high frequencies that don't belong. For polynomial nonlinearities, you can prove this is exact if the expanded bandwidth is large enough. ReLU and smooth activations still leave small residual artifacts, but the error is dramatically reduced compared to pointwise nonlinearities without expansion.

The deeper insight here is that the activation is no longer pointwise—it becomes nonlocal. By upsampling and downsampling, you're multiplying with filters and truncating frequency content, which couples information across space. This nonlocal structure is actually the key to making the architecture work. You're not just applying a function at each point; you're actively managing the frequency content of the entire field. This is how a neural operator can learn to be truly resolution-independent: the convolutions preserve band-limited structure by working continuously, and the nonlinearities accommodate the inevitable frequency growth by expanding and contracting the bandwidth in a controlled, mathematically justified way. The result is an architecture that can be trained on one resolution and tested faithfully on any other resolution satisfying the Nyquist barrier.
key_ideas: Band-limited functions (functions with a finite frequency cutoff) can be perfectly represented by discrete samples if the Nyquist barrier is satisfied—this means the gap between samples is small enough that no information is lost going from continuous to discrete and back.

Standard CNNs fail at resolution generalization because they apply fixed-size kernels to discrete grid points, making the network resolution-dependent—on a finer grid, the kernel hits different point values even for the same underlying function.

Pointwise nonlinearities (like ReLU applied to each grid point) create high frequencies that shouldn't exist in band-limited functions, corrupting the representation unless bandwidth is artificially expanded to accommodate them.

Representation equivalence means learning and discretization should commute—the architecture must ensure that projecting to finite dimensions, learning, and reconstructing up gives the same result as learning in infinite dimensions then discretizing.

Continuous convolutions with discrete kernels, combined with sync-based interpolation and resampling, allow the convolution operation to work on the underlying continuous function rather than the discrete grid.

Upsampling-nonlinearity-downsampling makes the activation function nonlocal and frequency-aware, deliberately expanding bandwidth before nonlinear operations then contracting back, which controls aliasing errors.

Practical implementation resizes test inputs back to the training resolution before applying the operator, using sync interpolation as the bridge between resolutions—this is not magical but a direct consequence of band-limited function theory.
WP02-hpKB-4.worked_intuition: Suppose you have a smooth temperature field represented on a 16-point grid. Training goes fine. At test time, you get a 32-point grid (finer resolution) of the same physical phenomenon. With a standard CNN: the kernel sees 3 points at positions (0.0, 0.5, 1.0) during training—it learns to map those specific values. On the finer grid, the same physical points are at (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0)—the kernel now hits different values, so it fails. With a convolutional operator: you take the 32-point values, use sync interpolation to lift them to a continuous function (band-limited to 16 frequencies because 32 points satisfy Nyquist for that band), then downsample them back to 16 points using the same interpolation. You now have values that represent the same continuous function on the original 16-point grid. The kernel applies, and you get a result that perfectly generalizes. The nonlinearity sits between upsample and downsample steps: if the intermediate output has 16 frequencies, you upsampled to 32, apply ReLU pointwise (which creates frequencies up to 32), then downsample back to 16, effectively filtering out the spurious high frequencies while keeping the physically meaningful ones.
WP02-hpKB-4.where_it_breaks: The theory assumes band-limited functions—if your PDE produces sharp discontinuities or high-frequency oscillations beyond your discretization, the method breaks. The Nyquist barrier must be respected; if you try a coarser grid than Nyquist allows, all bets are off. In practice, PDEs often have solutions that are not perfectly band-limited; the band limit must be large enough to capture all physically relevant scales. The upsampling factor in the nonlinearity is a design choice; doubling the bandwidth works well empirically but requires computational overhead—you cannot expand infinitely. For nonpolynomial nonlinearities like ReLU, residual high-frequency artifacts remain even after downsampling; the method is approximate, not exact, though the error is much smaller than pointwise approaches. On intricate, irregular geometries (not regular grids), the theory becomes harder to implement because resampling and interpolation are no longer straightforward.
WP02-hpKB-4.takeaway: Neural operators work across resolutions when you treat the underlying continuous functions and frequency content seriously, not the discrete grid points: use continuous convolutions with data resampling, expand bandwidth deliberately before nonlinearities to control aliasing, and rely on sync-based interpolation to bridge between representations—this architecture lets you train once and generalize to any resolution that satisfies the Nyquist condition.

Y3rvzsW8TVU.plain_title: How AI reads the molecular world: from protein sequences to 3D structures
Y3rvzsW8TVU.big_question: How can machine learning models learn to predict how proteins fold into 3D shapes and what molecules can do, starting only from text-like sequences of amino acids?
Y3rvzsW8TVU.everyday_anchor: Imagine if you had a recipe written in just letters (A, B, C, ... for each ingredient), and a neural network could learn from millions of recipes to guess not just what the final dish looks like, but also how it will taste and what it can be used for—that's what these models do with proteins.
walkthrough: The core problem that kicks off this whole field is a massive mismatch: proteins are built from just 20 naturally-occurring amino acids (the building blocks), strung together in long chains. But those chains fold into intricate 3D shapes that determine what the protein actually does—whether it speeds up a chemical reaction, holds your cells together, or carries oxygen in your blood. The challenge is that the sequence alone (the order of amino acids) doesn't obviously tell you the shape. Predicting this shape from sequence is like guessing the final form of origami from just a list of the color order of the paper—the spatial rules are hidden in the chemical properties of those amino acids, and you have to learn them from data.

For a long time, biologists had to use expensive experimental methods like X-ray crystallography or nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) to physically measure protein structures, which took months or years. But in 2020–2021, two breakthrough models emerged: AlphaFold and ESM. Both are transformer neural networks (the same architecture that powers modern language models). The insight is that protein sequences and natural language are analogous: both have a fixed vocabulary (20 amino acids vs. thousands of words), grammar-like rules, and long-range dependencies (amino acids far apart in the sequence can influence each other when folded). This analogy opened the door to applying deep learning methods from NLP to biology.

AlphaFold works by doing something clever: first, it searches genetic databases for similar sequences in other organisms and builds a multiple sequence alignment—a side-by-side comparison showing which positions are conserved (shared by many proteins) and which vary. Conserved positions hint at what's important for the protein to function. Alongside this, it generates a rough distance map between amino acids using known protein structures as templates. These two representations (the sequence alignment summary and the pairwise distance prediction) are fed into AlphaFold's core engine, which is a transformer with special 'attention' mechanisms that update both representations iteratively. Finally, a structure module converts the refined representations into actual 3D coordinates—distances between residues and bond angles. The model even recycles its own predictions, feeding the 3D output back as input to refine itself, typically three times. When AlphaFold competed in the 14th CASP (Critical Assessment of protein Structure Prediction) challenge, it achieved astonishing accuracy: predicting atom positions with a root mean square deviation of only 0.96 ångströms (a carbon atom is 1.4 ångströms wide).

ESM (Evolutionary Scale Modeling) took a different route. Meta's team trained a transformer on 250 million protein sequences using a self-supervised objective: they randomly masked some amino acids and asked the model to predict what was hidden. This is conceptually simple, but the model must learn deep biological knowledge to do it well. Remarkably, the hidden layer representations that ESM generates encode not just sequence information but also structural details. Researchers proved this by taking ESM's embeddings and training a simple logistic regression classifier to predict secondary structure elements (alpha helices and beta sheets) from the protein structure—achieving high accuracy. The key point: the model never saw 3D coordinates, only sequences, yet it learned structure-like patterns. Later, ESM was extended with a folding head (ESM-Fold), which uses the same recycling strategy as AlphaFold. ESM-Fold is about 60 times faster than AlphaFold because it doesn't need to search databases or compute multiple sequence alignments—it just takes a sequence and outputs a structure, working entirely standalone.

However, both AlphaFold and ESM-Fold have an important limitation: they predict a single, static 3D structure—typically the lowest-energy conformation. Real proteins are dynamic; they wiggle and bend. If you predict a structure and find that a known substrate doesn't fit in the enzyme's active site, it might be because the protein can actually flex open in reality but the model shows it closed. This limitation matters for drug discovery and enzyme engineering, where you need to understand not just the typical shape but the range of shapes a protein can adopt.

Beyond sequence-only models, the lecture introduces structure-based approaches. One method is 3D convolutional neural networks (3D-CNNs). These work by converting the 3D atomic coordinates into a 3D grid of voxels (imagine a 3D checkerboard). Each voxel gets assigned channel values based on what atoms are nearby: carbon atoms in one channel, nitrogen in another, oxygen in a third. Then standard convolutional operations scan this grid to extract features. This works well for small prediction tasks (like predicting whether a molecule will bind strongly to a protein), but has drawbacks: the model size grows cubically with grid resolution, much of the grid is empty space (sparse), and the model must be trained on multiple rotations of the protein to be rotation-invariant, making training expensive.

To handle protein structures more efficiently, the field is turning to graph neural networks (GNNs). A graph is a natural representation: atoms become nodes, chemical bonds become edges, and you can store properties on both. Unlike 3D grids, graphs don't waste memory on empty space. The model learns by letting information flow along edges—each atom learns features by aggregating information from its bonded neighbors, then passes refined information back. Transformers and message-passing GNNs use attention to learn which connections matter most. This approach is more memory-efficient, computationally scalable, and naturally equivariant to rotations, making it ideal for processing large numbers of molecular structures.

The lecture closes with the insight that multiple input modalities work: text-based (just sequences), structure-based (3D coordinates), and hybrid (structure + sequence together). For small molecules, chemists use SMILES—a linear text notation where atoms are chemical symbols, bonds are drawn with special characters, and rings are numbered. These can be tokenized and fed to transformers just like protein sequences. The field is discovering that different architectures and input types are useful for different questions. Self-supervised pretraining on massive unlabeled datasets (250 million sequences for ESM, vast SMILES corpora) followed by fine-tuning on smaller labeled datasets is becoming standard. This is how AI learns the molecular world: by finding patterns in billions of sequences and structures, learning a latent geometry of proteins and molecules, and using that knowledge to predict properties and design new ones.
key_ideas: Amino acid sequences alone don't reveal 3D protein shape; deep learning models learn this mapping from data by exploiting patterns (like conserved positions) and analogies to natural language (grammar, vocabulary, long-range dependencies).

AlphaFold combines sequence alignments, structural templates, attention mechanisms, and iterative refinement (recycling) to predict protein 3D coordinates with near-experimental accuracy; it's the most accurate but requires database searches, so it's slower.

ESM-Fold achieves similar accuracy 60× faster by using only sequence input and self-supervised pretraining on 250 million sequences, proving that structure information is encoded in sequence patterns even without seeing coordinates.

3D-CNNs can process protein structures as voxel grids (like 3D images) but are computationally expensive and struggle with sparsity and rotation invariance; graph neural networks are emerging as a more efficient alternative.

Graph neural networks represent proteins as atoms (nodes) and bonds (edges), avoiding grid sparsity and naturally handling rotations; they scale better for large datasets and are becoming the favored structure-based architecture.

Both text-based approaches (using sequence alone) and structure-based approaches (using 3D coordinates) are valuable; sequence methods are simpler and more data-rich, while structure methods capture spatial information crucial for tasks like drug binding prediction.

Self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled sequences (e.g., masked language modeling for ESM) learns deep biological knowledge; fine-tuning on small labeled datasets then enables specific predictions like function or stability.
Y3rvzsW8TVU.worked_intuition: Consider a small enzyme that naturally binds and processes molecule X. You want to engineer it to accept molecule Y instead. If you naively use only the amino acid sequence, you might miss the spatial constraints of the active site pocket. But if you predict the 3D structure with AlphaFold, you can visualize the pocket's shape and see that Y is too bulky. You might change one amino acid to make more room. Here's the AI part: instead of manually trying hundreds of mutations, you could use a GNN trained on many enzyme–substrate pairs to score which mutations are most likely to maintain protein stability while opening the pocket. The GNN learns 'which atoms talk to which' (the graph connectivity) and 'how changes propagate' (message passing), letting it predict the effect of a change without running expensive molecular simulations. This combines sequence knowledge (from pretraining like ESM), structure knowledge (from AlphaFold or a GNN encoder), and learned rules (from the training data).
Y3rvzsW8TVU.where_it_breaks: Both AlphaFold and ESM-Fold predict a single static structure, not the dynamic conformational ensemble proteins actually sample; so they fail if you need to know about flexible regions, transient binding pockets, or allosteric motion. They're also less reliable for very small proteins (< 50 residues) and multimeric assemblies (multiple subunits). Structure-based models like 3D-CNNs and GNNs require known 3D coordinates, which are far scarcer than sequences—so sequence-only methods scale better to unexplored proteins. Graph neural networks still require careful edge definition (which atoms count as bonded?), and they haven't yet matched the experimental accuracy of AlphaFold for backbone atoms. Finally, all these models are trained on experimentally solved structures, which are biased toward proteins that crystallize well or are easy to measure, not necessarily representative of the full proteome.
Y3rvzsW8TVU.takeaway: Neural networks learn to predict protein shape and molecular properties by finding patterns in massive amounts of sequence and structure data, using the insight that sequences encode structure just like natural language encodes meaning. The best modern approach layers methods: pretraining on huge unlabeled datasets to learn biology, then fine-tuning on small labeled datasets for specific tasks, and combining text-based speed with structure-based detail when possible.

YtJhReM5bHY.plain_title: Why Transformers Need Help to Learn Equations Efficiently
YtJhReM5bHY.big_question: Can we scale Transformers up to solve equations faster and better, or do they just need more data than existing methods?
YtJhReM5bHY.everyday_anchor: Imagine reading a page from a book—you don't compare every letter to every other letter. You focus on nearby words first, then connect those clusters together. That's what windowed attention does: it breaks the enormously expensive "look at everything at once" problem into manageable, overlapping local conversations.
walkthrough: When you have a Transformer and you want it to learn to solve a complicated equation (a PDE), the first thing you might try is to feed it the equation data directly. But there's a huge problem: standard Transformers compute 'attention'—a way of comparing every piece of information to every other piece. If you have 1,000 patches (pieces) of space to work with, you need 1,000 × 1,000 = one million comparisons. That's quadratic cost, and in 2D or 3D problems, it becomes nearly impossible. You can patch the data—chop your spatial domain into bigger chunks—to reduce the number of things being compared. Instead of comparing at the pixel level, you compare at the 16×16 patch level. But even that isn't enough. For problems in fluids or heat diffusion, the patches still represent too much averaged information, and you lose the detail you need.

The key insight is that you don't actually need global attention everywhere. Most of the physics is local—what happens at one spot depends mainly on nearby spots, not on a point far away on the other side of the domain. So instead of having every patch attend to every other patch, you divide the spatial domain into windows—larger blocks that contain many patches—and allow attention to happen only inside each window. This cuts the computation dramatically: now instead of quadratic in total patches, it's quadratic only within each window. If you have 4 × 4 patches in each window, the cost is manageable.

But now you face a new problem: if each window acts independently, information can't travel across window boundaries. Two nearby points on opposite sides of a window border have no path to talk to each other. The solution is elegant and simple: shift the windows in alternating layers. In layer 1, windows are aligned one way. In layer 2, you shift them by half a window size, so points that were on opposite sides of a border in layer 1 are now in the same window. In layer 3, you shift again. This way, over multiple layers, every point eventually gets to interact with its neighbors, but through a series of local conversations rather than one global one. This is called 'path length reduction'—information spreads through a chain of local connections rather than disappearing into unattended distance.

Beyond just attention, you need the Transformer's layers to process information at multiple scales simultaneously. Single-scale processing isn't expressive enough. Instead, the architecture (called a Swin Transformer or Scalable Operator Transformer) uses an encoder-decoder structure like a U-Net: the encoder coarsens the spatial resolution and increases the number of channels (features), processing the domain at progressively larger scales. The decoder then expands the resolution back down while reducing channels. At each scale, you do local Transformer processing. This is similar to how convolutional neural operators (CNOs) work—multiscale information helps you capture both large-scale patterns and fine details.

The challenge of scaling large Transformers is more than just architecture. When you increase the size of your model, you can run into problems with training: gradients don't flow as smoothly, and the optimization landscape becomes harder to navigate. The paper and this lecture discuss several small but important technical tricks: using cosine similarity instead of raw dot products for attention (which auto-normalizes), encoding position using relative distances on a log scale rather than absolute positions, and adjusting where layer normalization happens in the block. None of these alone is revolutionary, but together they help the model train more stably as you add more layers.

Despite all this engineering, the experiments show a sobering result: Transformers do not dramatically beat existing methods like Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) or Convolutional Neural Operators (CNO). On elliptic equations (steady-state problems), CNO is more sample-efficient than Transformers—it reaches good accuracy with fewer training examples. On time-dependent problems like the wave equation or Navier-Stokes, Transformers eventually scale better than FNO, but they're comparable to CNO, not orders of magnitude better. Transformers need a lot of data to shine. The smaller 20-million-parameter Transformer sometimes outperforms the 40-million-parameter version because there simply isn't enough training data to feed the larger model.

The real promise comes from a different direction: foundation models. The idea is to take your Transformer (or CNO) and pre-train it on a huge, diverse dataset of many PDEs—Navier-Stokes with different coefficients, reaction-diffusion equations, elliptic problems, time-dependent problems, all mixed together. This 200-million-parameter foundation model learns general patterns about how PDEs behave. Then, when you want to solve a specific new PDE, you don't start training from scratch. Instead, you fine-tune: take the pre-trained model and train it a little bit more on just a few new examples specific to your problem. The initial experiment is striking: where a standard Transformer needed 248 training samples to reach 3% error, a fine-tuned foundation model reaches the same error with 8 samples. This mirrors the success of large language models, which work best when you pre-train on internet-scale diverse data and then adapt to your specific task.

The honest takeaway is that Transformers with windowed attention and hierarchical structure are computationally viable and can work, but they are not a silver bullet. They require careful engineering to scale, they need lots of data to beat existing methods, and the gains are incremental rather than transformative. However, the foundation model approach—combining pre-training on diverse problems with fine-tuning on your specific case—is emerging as the most promising direction. This moves the field closer to how large language models have succeeded: learn broad patterns from scale and diversity, then specialize quickly with little task-specific data. But this is contemporary research, not yet fully understood, and represents the frontier of what's working right now.
key_ideas: Windowed attention: instead of comparing every piece of data to every other (quadratic cost), divide the domain into windows and do attention only within windows, then shift windows across layers so information can travel between them via overlapping connections.

Multiscale architecture: use an encoder-decoder structure to process information at coarse and fine scales simultaneously, capturing both large patterns and fine details, similar to existing convolutional neural operators.
Technical scaling tricks: cosine similarity, relative positional encoding on log scale, careful placement of layer normalization—small changes that improve training stability for very large models.

Empirical reality check: Transformers are not dramatically better than existing methods like CNO on most problems; they're competitive but data-hungry and need enough training examples to justify their added difficulty.

Foundation models as the path forward: pre-train on diverse PDEs at large scale, then fine-tune on your specific problem with few samples—this mirrors the success of large language models and shows the most promise for sample efficiency.

Data-model balance: there is a delicate equilibrium between how much data you have, how large your model is, and how well it will work. Too much model for too little data and the larger version actually performs worse than a smaller one.
Still an open frontier: the relationship between data scale, model size, and generalization in neural operator learning is not yet well understood and represents active contemporary research.
YtJhReM5bHY.worked_intuition: Picture a 4×4 grid of patches on a map. In layer 1 of your Transformer, you partition this into four 2×2 windows (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right), and attention happens only within each window. A patch in the top-left window cannot see into the top-right window. But in layer 2, you shift all windows by half a window width and height, so the boundaries move. Now, the patch that was isolated in the top-left corner of its window may now sit in the middle of a new 2×2 window with patches that include neighbors from what was previously unreachable. After a few layers of shifting, every patch has had a chance to mix with its neighbors through this chain of local windows. The cost at each layer is only 2×2 = 4 comparisons per window, times the number of windows (still manageable), whereas a single global attention layer would do 4×4 = 16 comparisons on every pair, and with thousands of patches that becomes intractable. This is why windowing plus shifting is so clever: it maintains the mixing power of Transformers while cutting computation from quadratic in total size to quadratic in window size.
YtJhReM5bHY.where_it_breaks: Transformers struggle when you have limited training data—they need orders of magnitude more examples than simpler methods like CNOs to reach the same accuracy on single-problem tasks. They also require careful tuning of architecture details (window size, number of layers, shifting patterns) and training tricks (optimizer choice, normalization placement) to work at scale. On small datasets typical of individual PDE problems, a CNN-based operator is often more sample-efficient. The method also doesn't solve the fundamental issue of training physics-informed neural networks—adding a physics loss term to the objective doesn't automatically make training easier or faster, and gradient propagation through differential operators remains numerically difficult. Finally, windowed Transformers lose the global receptive field that some problems might benefit from, and while alternating shifts help, they can't fully restore full-domain information mixing.
YtJhReM5bHY.takeaway: Windowed attention makes Transformers computationally feasible for spatial problems, but the real innovation is recognizing that scale and diversity matter more than a single clever architecture: pre-train a large model on many equations, then fine-tune it quickly on your specific problem, and you get the best of both worlds—expressivity from a huge model and sample efficiency from transfer learning.

ZhAxfuewf6s.plain_title: Building Reusable AI Models for Equations That Describe Nature
