walkthrough: Start with the big picture: almost all scientific code—fluid solvers, weather models, medical imaging pipelines—can be written as a composition of functions. You feed in numbers (vectors, tensors, matrices), apply operations sequentially, and get out answers. Mathematically it's just a vector function: input X becomes output Y through a chain of primitive operations like multiplication, sine, matrix solve. This matters because if the entire computation is differentiable, you can backpropagate gradients all the way through.

Automatic differentiation (autodiff) is the key enabler. It's what PyTorch and JAX do behind the scenes when you call loss.backward(). The machinery is elegant: decompose the Jacobian (the matrix of all partial derivatives) using the chain rule, then compute vector-Jacobian products in reverse mode. You don't need to build or store the full Jacobian matrix—you propagate a single "gradient vector" backwards through the computation graph, multiplying by each operation's local gradient as you go. The result: exact gradients, computed efficiently, without finite differences or symbolic math.

Now the hybrid idea: instead of replacing a physics solver with a neural network, embed a learnable network inside the solver. Real example: Navier-Stokes for fluid flow. The traditional numerical solver uses a coarse grid (fast, but loses accuracy to discretization error). Insert a neural network inside the time-stepping loop that learns a correction to make each coarse step look more like a fine-grid step. To train it, use autodiff to compute gradients of a loss function (like L2 distance to high-fidelity reference data) with respect to the network weights. The gradients flow backwards through both the solver and the network.

To make this work in practice, there are four steps. First, rewrite your traditional algorithm (probably Fortran or C++) into an autodiff approach like PyTorch or JAX. This is usually the hardest step because high-performance code is often intricate, but it unlocks the real wins. Second, open up the algorithm by inserting learnable components—maybe a correction network, maybe just a scalar parameter to learn. Third, collect training data: what you expect the outputs to be (real measurements or high-fidelity simulations). Fourth, train using gradient descent: compute the loss, backprop through the hybrid system, update weights.

A concrete example: the brachistochrone problem (what curve minimizes roll time?). A neural network parameterizes the curve shape. You don't feed the network training examples of the 'right' curve; instead, you minimize the actual quantity you care about—roll time. The network outputs a curve, a physics solver (using conservation of energy) computes the time, and autodiff gives you gradients with respect to the curve. You use autodiff twice: once to get the curve's slope (needed for the physics), and once to backprop the time loss. The network converges to the optimal curve (a cycloid) without ever seeing ground-truth labels. The loss function is derived from physics, not from labeled data.

Another use case: inverse problems like computed tomography. You have X-ray measurements (a sinogram) and want to recover the internal image. Traditionally, this is solved by gradient descent: guess an image, simulate the sinogram, compare to measurements, compute gradients, and update. But the forward simulation (radon transform) can be expensive, and the loss landscape is non-convex with many local minima—gradient descent gets stuck. Hybrid fix: train a neural network to predict a better step than naive gradient descent. At each iteration, the network ingests the gradient of the loss (what gradient descent would do), the current image, and maybe regularization scores, and outputs a smarter update direction. This is learned from many trial inverse problems: run gradient descent on synthetic data with known truth, collect the trajectory, and train the network to predict better steps.

The memory trade-off in autodiff is subtle but important. Reverse-mode autodiff (backprop) must store all intermediate activations from the forward pass, so memory grows linearly with the depth of computation. Forward-mode autodiff (propagating sensitivities forward) doesn't need to store intermediate states and uses constant memory, but it must run once per output dimension you want gradients for. In scientific computing where you have millions of parameters but a scalar loss, reverse mode is standard. In contrast to misconceptions: autodiff is not symbolic differentiation (you don't manipulate equations) and not finite differences (you get exact gradients, not approximations).

The philosophical shift: by embedding learned components directly into physics, you're admitting uncertainty while using structure. If you knew all the physics perfectly, you wouldn't need the network. If you knew nothing, a pure neural network might work but needs huge data. Hybrid methods split the difference: 'Here's what we know is true (the conservation laws, the geometry), and here's what we'll learn (the parameterization, the closure term, the discretization correction).' The result generalizes better and trains faster than either extreme, because the network only learns what physics doesn't already tell you.
key_ideas: Scientific code is differentiable composition of functions. Any program written as a chain of operations (solves, simulations, integrals) can have gradients computed through it using autodiff, because each step is differentiable.

Autodiff via reverse mode computes exact gradients by backpropagating a 'gradient vector' through the computation graph. Memory cost is linear in depth. Forward mode has constant memory but must run multiple times for multiple outputs.

Hybrid workflows insert learnable neural networks inside traditional physics solvers (not replacing them). The network learns to correct, accelerate, or improve parts the solver handles poorly, then the whole thing is trained end-to-end with autodiff.

Loss functions come from physics, not labels. Instead of feeding the network training pairs, you compute a physically meaningful loss (travel time, image error, simulation accuracy) and backprop through both the physics and the network.

Inverse problems are hard because they are underdetermined and noisy. A hybrid approach can learn to take smarter steps than gradient descent by observing the loss landscape in context, replacing naive descent with a learned optimizer.

Four-step recipe: (1) rewrite physics code in autodiff approach, (2) insert learnable components, (3) gather training data, (4) train end-to-end with backprop. This works because autodiff handles the chain rule automatically.

The hybrid approach is a confession and a strength: 'Here's what we know (physics), here's what we'll learn (the unknown part).' Generalizes better than pure neural nets, trains faster than pure solvers.
h8BH-6tjecc.worked_intuition: Take the brachistochrone example step by step. (1) Define a neural network that takes X-position and outputs Y-position of the curve. (2) For a given curve shape, compute the actual travel time using conservation of energy: v = sqrt(2gy), and integrate distance/speed along the curve. (3) Use torch.autograd.grad to compute dy/dx (the slope of the curve) by differentiating the network's output with respect to X. (4) Plug dy/dx and y into the travel-time integral formula. (5) Use torch.trapezoid to approximate the integral as a sum. (6) Call loss.backward() to backprop the travel time with respect to the network weights. (7) Take an optimizer step. After many iterations, the network converges to the cycloid shape that actually minimizes time. The key insight: you never showed the network what the answer looks like. You only told it what quantity to minimize, and the physics did the rest.
h8BH-6tjecc.where_it_breaks: Hybrid methods inherit the brittleness of physics solvers: if the solver fails (diverges, requires tiny timesteps), backprop fails with it. The network can't learn if the forward model is broken. Also, if the physics is wrong, the network learns to compensate but can't generalize beyond the data regime it saw. Scalability: in very high dimensions (turbulence, climate) or with very expensive solvers, the cost of running the solver many times (once per gradient step) can dominate. If the loss landscape is extremely non-convex, the network's learned updates might help but can still get stuck in local minima, especially if the network architecture doesn't match the problem structure. Finally, interpretability: a learned correction inside a physics solver is harder to debug than either a pure solver or a pure neural network.
h8BH-6tjecc.takeaway: Hybrid workflows are a way to blend learning and physics: keep the structure you trust (conservation laws, numerical methods), teach the network to fix what you don't understand, and use autodiff to wire them together. The network learns not from labeled examples but from minimizing what you actually care about—time, error, energy, or any objective derived from the physics.

jnjYsm4NjhE.plain_title: Teaching Neural Networks to Act Like Differential Equations
jnjYsm4NjhE.big_question: What if we put neural networks inside differential equations to learn unknown physics, and what does that teach us about how neural networks themselves work? How can viewing neural networks as equation solvers help us design better architectures?
jnjYsm4NjhE.everyday_anchor: Imagine trying to predict how a predator and prey population change over time. Instead of writing down the exact rules (which you only partly understand), you write a partial rule with a neural network filling in the blanks. The neural network learns what you didn't know. But here's the surprise: this idea reveals that ResNets (a standard neural network type) are secretly just solving differential equations one small step at a time.
walkthrough: The lecture starts with a concrete problem: we have real data showing predator and prey populations rising and falling over time, but the traditional equations we use to model this rely on simplifying assumptions that rarely hold in nature. Instead of guessing all the coefficients in our equations, what if we let a neural network learn the parts we don't understand? This is the core idea of a neural differential equation (NDE). You write down the structure you're confident about (e.g., 'the prey population changes based on predator population') but replace the exact function with a neural network that learns from data.

To actually solve an NDE, we use the same numerical methods as for regular differential equations. The simplest is Euler's method: break time into tiny steps, and at each step, ask the neural network 'what happens next?' and update the populations. This is simple to code: a for loop where inside each iteration you call the neural network. Crucially, because the entire forward pass (running the solver) is differentiable, you can use automatic differentiation to train the neural network by comparing its predictions to real data. The solver outputs the full trajectory through time, and you optimize the neural network weights to match what you actually observed.

Here's where it gets interesting. When you draw out the Euler solver as a diagram—showing how you take the current state, run it through the neural network, scale by a tiny time step, and add it back to the state—it looks exactly like a residual connection in a ResNet. That skip connection (adding input to output) is the same as the 'keep what you have and add a small change' principle of numerical integration. This means ResNets with millions of parameters are, in the limit of infinitely many thin layers, just solving a differential equation. Training a ResNet weights means learning the right-hand side of an ODE. This is a profound bridge between physics and machine learning: the architecture you use for image classification is secretly a discretized differential equation solver.

You can generalize this insight. Different numerical solvers (Runge-Kutta, implicit methods) produce different computational graphs, which are different neural network architectures. A 1D convolution layer, when stacked infinitely, solves a specific partial differential equation (PDE). This means you can ask the inverse question: what PDE does a given architecture solve? And more practically: if you know your data has oscillatory behavior, you could design a neural network based on the differential equation for coupled oscillators, giving it a physics-informed inductive bias without hand-coding features.

The lecture demonstrates this with human activity recognition. A smartwatch records acceleration (X, Y, Z components) while a person walks up stairs. Instead of using a generic LSTM or GRU, the researchers designed an RNN cell based on the coupled harmonic oscillator equation—the dynamics of multiple masses connected by springs. The hidden state represents the displacement and velocity of these coupled oscillators, and the network learns the spring constants and damping coefficients from data. When they plot what the hidden state does over time, it shows beautiful coupled oscillations, giving insight into what the network learned. Remarkably, this physics-inspired architecture works well not only on oscillatory data but also on non-oscillatory datasets like sentiment classification, suggesting the inductive bias generalizes.

A key insight emerges from comparing different approaches. If you tried to predict populations by training a neural network on time alone (ignoring the underlying differential equation), it would memorize the training data but fail badly on times it hasn't seen. But an NDE trained on one full cycle of oscillation generalizes much further because the network only ever sees inputs in its training range (the phase space is bounded), so any new time query falls back on inputs the network has encountered before. The structure of the differential equation—assuming a first-order rate-of-change form—adds strong physics constraints that prevent overfitting. This is why NDEs generalize so much better than naive neural networks on dynamical systems.

The distinction between NDEs and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) matters. A PINN uses a neural network to approximate the solution to a differential equation (the output is the solution). An NDE puts a neural network inside the differential equation itself (the neural network is part of the right-hand side). So an NDE solver is a hybrid method: it's a numerical integrator with learned components. This opens a design space: you can keep parts of your equation fixed (because you're confident in the physics) and let neural networks learn only the mysterious pieces. You can also think of NDEs as surrogate models—they learn to mimic expensive simulators by learning the dynamics directly.

The training process is straightforward but effective. You start with initial conditions (known from your data), run the NDE solver forward in time, and compare the entire trajectory to observations. Automatic differentiation flows gradients through the entire solver, updating the neural network weights to minimize the difference. This works for very long time horizons because the solver is deterministic and differentiable. The neural network doesn't need to memorize a long sequence; it learns a compact representation of the dynamics that generates long sequences correctly. This is why NDEs are so sample-efficient compared to opaque model sequence models.
key_ideas: Neural Differential Equations embed learnable neural networks into differential equations, replacing unknown physics with learned functions while keeping the known structure intact.
Residual Networks (ResNets) are, in the continuous limit, just Euler solvers for differential equations—each residual block is one time step of numerical integration.
Different numerical methods (Euler, Runge-Kutta, implicit) correspond to different neural network architectures, so you can use knowledge of PDEs to design better neural networks.
NDEs generalize far beyond their training time horizon because they learn dynamics (the rules), not solutions (the answers), staying within the bounded phase space the network has seen.

By designing neural networks from differential equations that match your data (e.g., coupled oscillators for rhythmic signals), you inject physics domain knowledge without hard-coding features, improving both accuracy and interpretability.
jnjYsm4NjhE.worked_intuition: Consider predicting the motion of a pendulum swinging back and forth. A standard neural network trained on time values (0.0, 0.1, 0.2 seconds) to predict angle can nail the training interval but will be garbage at t=2.0 seconds because it only memorized angles for those specific times. An NDE learns the pendulum equation instead. It learns 'the acceleration is proportional to the negative angle (gravity pulling back)' and a damping term. Once trained on one swing cycle (0 to 5 seconds), it can predict 100 seconds forward because it's computing new positions from current position and velocity every tiny time step, following the learned dynamics. The hidden state (position and velocity) stays bounded between -90 and +90 degrees, so the network only queries inputs it has effectively seen during training. If you plot the learned hidden state over long time, you see the sinusoidal oscillations decay due to damping—the network's learned representation of the physics.
jnjYsm4NjhE.where_it_breaks: NDEs struggle with truly chaotic systems where tiny changes in initial conditions lead to wildly different long-term futures (sensitive dependence). They also require good physics assumptions; if you pick the wrong base equation (e.g., coupled oscillators for non-oscillatory data), you've added constraints that harm performance. Very long-term forecasting is still hard because small numerical errors in the solver accumulate. NDEs also require differentiable solvers, so you can't use adaptive step-size solvers (which are conditional and hard to backpropagate through) without special techniques. Finally, the interpretability benefit only works if your base equation is meaningful; wrapping a opaque model neural network in an ODE that gets discretized as an RNN doesn't magically make the weights interpretable, just more constrained.
jnjYsm4NjhE.takeaway: Neural networks aren't just function approximators—they're fundamentally discretized differential equation solvers. By recognizing this, you can reverse-engineer better architectures from physical principles, make neural networks more sample-efficient on dynamical data, and gain insight into what hidden states actually represent. The same idea works in both directions: classical numerical methods inspire neural network design, and neural network innovations (like attention) can suggest new ways to solve PDEs.

lEUgPvDi5O8.plain_title: Operator Learning in Practice: From Data to Downstream Tasks
lEUgPvDi5O8.big_question: Once you have trained a neural network to act as a surrogate (fast predictor) for a physics simulation, how do you actually use it for real engineering goals like design optimization or uncertainty quantification? And what are the practical pitfalls?
lEUgPvDi5O8.everyday_anchor: Imagine you can train a small neural network to predict the lift and drag on an airplane wing 100× faster than actually running a CFD simulation. Now you want to use that fast predictor to find the best wing shape—or to understand what happens when your measurements have uncertainty. These downstream tasks reveal the real value of the surrogate, but also hidden challenges.
walkthrough: The last lecture showed that you can build a neural network surrogate to learn the solution operator—the map from input (like wing design parameters) to output (like lift and drag). But knowing how to predict is only the beginning. The real payoff comes from using those predictions for actual engineering decisions: designing better shapes, quantifying how uncertain your inputs translate into uncertain outputs, or controlling a system. This lecture walks through two major downstream applications and why naive approaches fail.

The first big application is uncertainty quantification, or UQ—understanding the distribution of outputs when inputs have uncertainty. Real-world flows don't happen at exactly one angle of attack or one Mach number; they occur within ranges. If you know the incoming flow has a 5% uncertainty range, how does that ripple through to the lift and drag you care about? The classical answer is Monte Carlo: sample the input distribution thousands of times, run your simulation each time, collect the outputs, and compute statistics. The problem is obvious: if each simulation takes 40 minutes and you need 10,000 samples to get decent uncertainty estimates, you are spending months of computing.

Here is where the trained surrogate becomes magical. You can take a modest number of carefully chosen training samples (say, 128 shaped using Sobol or Halton sequences—low-discrepancy point sets that fill the parameter space more evenly than random points), train your neural network once (an hour of work), and then run 100,000 evaluations through that network in a second. Each network forward pass takes microseconds. You get two orders of magnitude speedup even compared to quasi-Monte Carlo. This works because the map from inputs to outputs has structure (bounded mixed derivatives, no discontinuities) that the network can capture, and that structure allows you to use cleverly spaced training points instead of random ones.

The second major application is design optimization under constraints—the problem that really motivates much of aerospace. You want to find the wing parameters that minimize drag while keeping lift fixed and respecting manufacturing constraints. Mathematically, you need gradients: you set up a loss function (minimize drag, penalize lift deviation, penalize structural violations), then use gradient descent to find better designs. But computing gradients the classical way—solving the full forward simulation for each step, then solving an 'adjoint' PDE to back out the gradient—is ferociously expensive. Each gradient step in 2D takes an hour or more; in 3D, a day or more. You might need thousands of steps. The solution: replace the expensive simulation with your trained neural network, compute gradients via automatic differentiation (backprop), and optimize. Now each gradient step is fast enough that you can afford many steps and find good designs.

However, there is a subtle trap. When you train your network, you spread training samples uniformly across the design space using Sobol or random sampling. But optimal designs do not live at random places in that space; they cluster along certain curves and manifolds—where gradients align, where constraints are active, where the physics creates sweet spots. If you train only with random or uniform samples, your network will be less accurate exactly where the optima are. This means your gradients are biased, and you find suboptimal designs. The fix requires active learning: start with coarse training, solve the optimization, find candidate optima, add those regions to your training set, retrain, and repeat. This way you adaptively concentrate data where it matters.

The lecture demonstrates this with a 2D airfoil shape optimization. Using passive training (uniformly sampled), you might find a lift-to-drag ratio of 100; the true optimum is closer to 200. With active learning, you get the factor-of-2 improvement. But more remarkably, the improvement in absolute terms is striking: the reference design had a drag coefficient of 115; the optimized design achieves 58—cutting drag in half with only tiny visible shape changes. No human designer could tweak the shape that finely by hand; this is precisely why automated design matters.

All this success rests on one deep assumption: that the parameterization itself is well-chosen and unique. Here is where the narrative breaks and the lecture introduces the crisis of the field. A single physics—the quadratic function y=x²—can be parameterized one way (one input x) or rewritten as y = 0.5·(A₁x + B₁) + 0.5·(A₂x + B₂) with four parameters. The same mathematical function is represented differently. If you train a network to learn the function from one parameter and then ask it to work with the four-parameter version, it fails completely—it does not realize it is the same underlying map. This non-uniqueness of parameterization destroys generalization. Worse, hand-crafting parameterizations (like the Hicks–Henne basis functions for wings) requires decades of engineering intuition. For a new design problem—a custom drone, an unusual material—there is no parameterization waiting to be used. You must invent one from scratch, and you cannot be sure it is ideal.

This generalization failure is not a minor academic quibble; it is the central crisis motivating the entire shift to operator learning. The next lectures will abandon hand-crafted, finite-dimensional parameterizations and work directly with functions—infinite-dimensional entities that live in their own Banach spaces. Rather than choosing how to represent a shape as a vector of 20 parameters, you represent it as a function, and you train networks that take functions as input and output functions. This is harder to implement and reason about, but it breaks free of the parameterization trap. A Fourier operator network or DeepONet learns the operator in a way that is insensitive to how you discretize or parameterize the underlying physics.
key_ideas: Surrogates enable downstream tasks—once you have a fast, accurate neural network predictor, you can use its gradient to optimize (find best designs), propagate uncertainty (quantify risk), or solve inverse problems (infer inputs from observations)—at a tiny fraction of the simulation cost

Low-discrepancy sampling (Sobol, Halton sequences) beats random sampling for training in moderate-to-high dimensions because they spread points more evenly; error decays as 1/n instead of 1/√n, yielding 10–100× fewer samples needed for the same accuracy

Active learning for optimization: training data should concentrate where optima live, not uniformly across the space; iteratively retraining with samples from intermediate optima dramatically improves design quality

Parameterization is not unique and not innocent: the same underlying map (wing shape, material profile) can be represented as functions of 1, 2, 4, or 100 parameters; a network trained in one parameterization fails to generalize to another, breaking the entire learning promise

Finite-dimensional parameterizations require domain expertise (decades of engineering intuition for airfoils) and do not exist for novel problems; this motivates abandoning hand-tuned vectors in favor of infinite-dimensional function spaces and true operator learning
lEUgPvDi5O8.worked_intuition: Suppose you optimize an airfoil using gradient descent on a surrogate neural network trained with 128 carefully chosen sample airfoils. Each step: (1) propose a tiny shape change, (2) evaluate lift and drag via the network (10 microseconds), (3) backprop to get the gradient of drag with respect to each design parameter, (4) take a gradient step downhill. After 100 steps, you find a design that reduces drag by 50%, with shape changes so small no human could hand-draw them. Compare this to the traditional process: generate training samples (128 × 40 minutes = 80 hours CPU), train network (1 hour), optimize with the network (microseconds per step, hundreds of steps = still microseconds). Total: roughly 80 hours of setup, then unlimited fast optimization. The traditional all-simulation approach: 100 optimization steps × 1 hour per adjoint solve = 100 hours, with far coarser designs found. The surrogate wins by a factor of 50 in this problem.
lEUgPvDi5O8.where_it_breaks: This works only in bounded regimes where the physics is smooth and well-parametrized. It breaks when: (1) you venture far outside the training region (the network was not trained there and extrapolates poorly); (2) the problem has sharp transitions or shocks in unexpected places (e.g., flow separation at an unusual angle—the network was trained on smooth examples); (3) you care about rare events or tail risk, because Monte Carlo needs exponentially more samples as events get rarer (though surrogates help); (4) the parameterization is hidden or non-obvious (e.g., you have 100 design variables but only 10 degrees of physical freedom—you are overfitting a constrained space, and the network cannot discover the true structure); and most fundamentally, (5) if you parameterize differently (e.g., wing as 20 parameters vs. 50 parameters), your network does not transfer, breaking the promise of learning the underlying operator.
lEUgPvDi5O8.takeaway: Trained surrogates unlock fast downstream tasks (optimization, UQ, inverse problems) and can be 50–100× faster than traditional approaches, but only if your parameterization is well-chosen, consistent, and fits the problem. The next frontier is operator learning on function spaces directly—replacing 'learn a map from 20 numbers to a number' with 'learn a map from a function to a function'—to break free of the parameterization bottleneck.

lXH0jlbm7z8.plain_title: Learning physical rules that work at any resolution with Fourier Neural Operators
lXH0jlbm7z8.big_question: How can we teach a neural network to learn the deep rules of a physical system (described by differential equations) in a way that works whether we sample it at 64 points or 128 points — or any other resolution?
lXH0jlbm7z8.everyday_anchor: Imagine you have a video of a fluid swirling. A good prediction model shouldn't care if you show it a low-resolution video or a high-resolution video — it should know the actual physics of how fluids move, not just memorize a specific grid of numbers. That's the problem we're solving.
walkthrough: For the last two lectures, we tried teaching neural networks to solve differential equations directly using physics constraints. That failed because there are too many limitations. So we switched strategy: use real data and let the network learn from examples of input-to-output pairs. But we face a fundamental mismatch. A differential equation is an operator — a mapping from one infinite-dimensional function space to another. If I give it a different initial condition, I get a new solution. But standard neural networks only know how to map from finite vectors to finite vectors. If I train one on 256 numbers (a grid), it learns exactly that grid. Change the grid size to 512 or 128, and it breaks. This isn't just inefficiency — it means the network didn't actually learn the operator at all; it memorized a specific discrete representation.

The first idea was to use convolutional neural networks. Convolutions are clever: instead of a dense weight matrix connecting every input to every output, you use a small sliding kernel that moves across the domain. This kernel is the same everywhere you apply it. When you discretize a PDE on a grid, nearby points matter more than distant ones — fluids don't care about the exact grid spacing, only about relative positions. A CNN respects this locality. Better yet, you can train it on a 64×64 grid, then slide that same learned kernel across a 128×128 grid. Computation scales, and the model is actually shift-invariant — exactly what we want for a true operator. But when we tested this on Navier-Stokes flows, something terrible happened: train on 64×64 with 5% error, test on 32×32, and suddenly the error jumps to 25%. Change to 128×128, same explosion. The network hadn't learned the flow physics — it learned the discrete 64×64 representation. A PDE solution is a function, not a 4,096-dimensional vector. So our goal remains unsolved.

The real insight is to flip the problem: instead of discretizing the problem first (infinite → finite) then learning (finite domains), we do the opposite. Make the neural network itself infinite-dimensional from the start, then discretize only at the end for computation. This is called a neural operator. We extend each piece of a standard neural network to function spaces. Normally, a neural network layer is a matrix-vector multiply: output = A·input + b, where A is a learnable weight matrix and b is a bias vector. To lift this to functions, we replace the matrix-vector product with a kernel integral operator: output(x) = ∫ k(x,y) · input(y) dy + bias_function(x), where k is a learned kernel and the bias is now a learned function. The activation function is applied pointwise to the output at every location. This is mathematically clean and canonical — it's the obvious generalization of finite-dimensional neural networks to function spaces.

But here's the catch: computing those integrals naively is expensive. For each point x, you have to sum over all n points in the domain. That's n² operations per layer. With 10,000 points? 100 million operations per layer. With several layers, this becomes impossible. Around 2020, Zongyi Li and collaborators had a brilliant observation: physical systems have translation invariance. The laws of physics don't depend on where you stand. So the kernel k(x,y) only depends on the difference x−y, which means it's a convolution. Convolutions are expensive in physical space — but incredibly cheap in frequency space. In frequency space, convolution becomes multiplication. So here's the trick: take a Fourier transform of your input function to get its frequency content, multiply by a learned matrix in frequency space (O(n log n) with FFT), then take an inverse Fourier transform back to physical space. Because you only keep a fixed number of frequencies (say, 30 modes) — independent of grid resolution — the learnable part doesn't blow up when you change resolution. The Fourier transform itself is a fixed operation, not learned.

The full FNO layer works like this. You start with an input function sampled at n grid points. First, you lift it to a higher-dimensional feature space (channel mixing) by applying a learned matrix at each point independently — this is just a change of coordinates, not resolution-dependent. Then you take the discrete Fourier transform of these features, which produces a fixed number of frequency modes (e.g., 30, whether you have 64 points or 128). You multiply by a learnable weight matrix in frequency space, which mixes the frequencies together. You take the inverse Fourier transform to get back to the n points in physical space. Finally, you apply a pointwise activation function (ReLU or tanh). You repeat this Fourier layer several times, and at the end you project back down to your desired output channels. The magic is that the learnable matrix depends only on the number of frequency modes and channels — not the number of grid points. So you can apply the trained network to any resolution.

In principle, this solves the resolution problem: train on 64×64, test on 32×32, 128×128, or any size. But when the lecturer tried this on Navier-Stokes, something interesting appeared. At the training resolution (64×64), the error was 3.5%, excellent. But when going to higher resolution (super-resolution), the error crept up slightly. When going to lower resolution (sub-resolution), the error rose noticeably, though much less than with CNNs (which saw 25% jumps). Why doesn't it work perfectly? The reason is that the frequencies are cut off. A 64×64 grid can represent frequencies up to a limit; if the true solution has energy in frequencies beyond that cutoff, truncating them loses information. When you go to a finer grid, you can resolve those high frequencies, and the network has to make do without them. For smooth solutions of PDEs, high frequencies are naturally damped, so the error is small. But the network hasn't learned the true operator — it's learned a filtered, truncated version of it. This is an honest limitation, not a bug in the method.

FNO works well in practice because real PDEs naturally filter out high frequencies. Diffusion, viscosity, and other smoothing effects suppress noise and fine-scale wiggling. So even though theoretically the network sees a filtered problem, for physically realistic solutions the filter doesn't matter much. Mathematically, we can prove that FNO is a universal approximator of operators — just like standard neural networks are universal function approximators. If the true operator is continuous, FNO with enough layers and modes can approximate it arbitrarily well. But this is a theoretical guarantee; in practice, you still need to train on representative data, and you'll see the resolution-generalization issue for pathological operators (like random shuffling), even with FNO. The key insight is that FNO shifts the bottleneck from being resolution-dependent to being frequency-dependent, which is a huge practical win for physics-based learning.
key_ideas: Operator learning: Learn a mapping from one function space to another, not just from vectors to vectors. The learned rule should apply at any grid resolution.
Kernel integral operators: The infinite-dimensional analog of matrix-vector multiplication; convolve an input function with a learned kernel. Expensive naively, but manageable in frequency space.
Translation invariance: Physical laws don't depend on position, so the kernel only depends on differences. This turns expensive convolution into learnable multiplication in Fourier space.

Fixed frequency cutoff: FNO uses a fixed number of Fourier modes (e.g., 30) regardless of grid size. This makes the learnable parameters independent of resolution, enabling smooth evaluation at different grids.
FFT efficiency: Fourier transform of n points takes O(n log n) time with FFT. Naive quadratic kernel operations become linear in practice.
Residual learning: Training the difference between output and input (when they're in the same space) stabilizes learning and is applied throughout FNO.

Limitations and honesty: FNO works well for smooth, filtered solutions of PDEs where high frequencies don't matter. For pathological operators with full high-frequency content, resolution generalization still degrades. It's not magic, but a smart trade-off that matches the structure of physical problems.
lXH0jlbm7z8.worked_intuition: Consider the Navier-Stokes equation for a 2D fluid flow. You have an initial velocity field, and you want to predict the velocity at some later time. Normally, you'd sample the velocity on a 64×64 grid (4,096 numbers), feed it into an MLP that outputs 4,096 numbers at the next time step. If you then try a 128×128 grid, the MLP fails because it expects exactly 4,096 inputs. With FNO: (1) Sample the velocity on any grid, say 64×64. (2) Lift it to 16 channels per point (learning better coordinates). (3) Fourier transform each channel across space — you get 32 frequency modes (fixed, chosen once). (4) Multiply a learned 16×16 matrix that mixes the 32 modes at each frequency (learnable part). (5) Inverse Fourier transform back to 64 spatial points. (6) Apply ReLU pointwise. Repeat a few times. (7) Project back to 2 velocity components. Output is a velocity field on the 64×64 grid. Now test on 128×128: the first step gives you a lifted field at 128 points. The Fourier transform produces the same 32 frequency modes. The learned matrix still applies (it doesn't know or care about 64 vs 128). Inverse transform goes back to 128 spatial points. The activation and projection are pointwise, so they work at any grid size. The network literally doesn't see the difference in resolution — it only sees frequency modes and channels.
lXH0jlbm7z8.where_it_breaks: FNO is not truly resolution-invariant for all operators. The fixed frequency cutoff causes information loss when you evaluate at finer grids. High-frequency features that weren't present in the training data are ignored. For 'pathological' operators with no natural smoothing (like random permutations of points), FNO fails just as badly as CNNs when you change resolution. The theoretical guarantee of universal approximation doesn't guarantee that the network will *learn* the true operator — only that it *could* in principle if given enough layers, modes, and training. In practice, you need the operator to be 'nice' (e.g., smooth, with damped high frequencies) for the frequency truncation to not hurt generalization. Also, FNO is most natural on regular Cartesian grids. On irregular grids or non-Euclidean domains, you'd need to adapt the Fourier machinery significantly, or use other operator learning methods.
lXH0jlbm7z8.takeaway: The real advance in FNO is making the learnable parameters independent of grid resolution by working in frequency space instead of physical space. You get a network that can be trained on one resolution and applied to any other, and it stays accurate when the underlying physics naturally suppresses high frequencies — which is almost all the PDEs we care about in science and engineering. It's not perfect operator learning, but it's close enough for real problems, and it's become the standard baseline.

u1KFcAvjyCI.plain_title: How to teach neural networks to predict how things change over time
u1KFcAvjyCI.big_question: When you have a movie (or time-series data) of a changing system, how do you build a neural network that can generate a whole trajectory into the future, not just one snapshot? And how do you actually train it without errors piling up?
u1KFcAvjyCI.everyday_anchor: Imagine you train a weather model to predict tomorrow's weather from today's. That's easy. But then at inference, if you want to predict next week's weather, you feed your prediction back in, over and over. Each small mistake grows. You're essentially asking: how do you build a model that can keep going for hundreds of steps without spiraling into nonsense?
walkthrough: First, let's be clear about what the problem actually is. In previous lectures, you learned about operator learning: taking an initial condition (like a snapshot of a fluid flow) and predicting the solution at one specific later time. That's clean: you give one image, you get one image back. But real time-dependent problems are messier. In nature and in computers, time flows forward in discrete steps. When you simulate the Navier-Stokes equations, you don't just compute the final state—you march forward hour by hour, frame by frame, and at each step you save a snapshot. What you actually have is a video: a sequence of images with time baked in. The natural form of scientific data is trajectories, not isolated pairs.

Here's the key insight from causality: in a time-dependent system, you can compose solutions. If I know how the system evolves from time zero to time T, and separately from time T to time 2T, I can chain them together to get from zero to 2T. This is the semigroup property. It means that time gives the system a direction—you can always march forward, but not always backward (only reversible systems go backward). This matters because it suggests we could train on short steps and reuse them, like a numerical solver does. But there's a catch.

The naive approach would be to build K different neural operators, each one predicting the solution at a different time level. Operator one predicts the state at t=0.1, operator two at t=0.2, and so on. This is horrifying: you need hundreds of models. And worse, you're not using the fact that you already know the state at t=0.1—you could use that to predict t=0.2. You'd be throwing away information. So this approach fails immediately.

What people actually do is autoregressive evaluation, also called rollout. You train one operator to predict the next frame given the current frame, and at test time you apply it repeatedly: feed in the initial condition, get frame 1; feed in frame 1, get frame 2; feed in frame 2, get frame 3. Like a language model that generates one word at a time. During training, since each small prediction problem is the same (delta T is fixed and uniform), you can just use supervised learning. This is seductive because it looks like standard next-frame prediction, and it's what 80-90% of papers do. The operator doesn't even need to know about time—it just takes one image and produces the next one, and the time step is implicit.

But there are three serious problems with rollout. First: error accumulation. Each neural network prediction has some error—maybe 1% on a single frame. When you chain 50 predictions together, errors compound. You start with clean initial conditions from summer, predict forward frame by frame, and by frame 50 you're giving predictions for winter. The model was trained on summer weather, so summer errors accumulate into impossible weather. The error isn't random—it's biased, because the model has never seen the regime it's being asked to predict into. You could try to train on longer rollouts to fix this, but then backpropagation through 50 steps hits the exploding/vanishing gradient problem: gradients either shrink to zero or blow up, and learning breaks.

Second: you're limited to discrete time. You can only evaluate at the exact time points in your training data. If your data has frames at t=0, 0.1, 0.2, ..., you can only predict at those points. Real PDEs are continuous in time—there's no reason you shouldn't be able to predict at t=0.157. Third: you're not actually using the trajectory data as richly as you could. In your training set, for each initial condition, you have all K frames. But rollout training only uses the pairs (frame i, frame i+1). You're ignoring the structure that frame 0 → frame K uniquely determines how frames 0 → 1 → 2 → ... → K evolve together.

The solution is time conditioning. Instead of hiding time and learning an implicit time step, you make time explicit as an input to the network. Time becomes another channel, like temperature or pressure. So your operator takes: the initial condition (an image) and the time you want the solution at, and outputs the solution at that time. This sounds simple, but there's a subtlety. If you just concatenate time once at the input and send it through a 20-layer network, by layer 10 the network has effectively forgotten about the time value—it's been processed and mixed away. So instead of giving time once, you condition every layer on time. This is done through conditional normalization. Every layer in the network has a batch-norm or layer-norm step. Normally, normalization rescales the intermediate values to have mean zero and unit variance. But in time-conditioned networks, you also apply a learnable transformation that depends on time. So the normalization at layer 3 is different from the normalization at layer 4 if you're asking for a different time. Mathematically, you're adding time-dependent matrices and biases to the normalization—typically learned by small neural networks. The effect is that time drips through the entire network, modulating how features are normalized at each step.

Here's what you gain: now you can actually train on the full trajectory. Given one initial condition and its trajectory (frames 0 through K), you can create training pairs like (initial condition, t=0.1) → frame at 0.1, (initial condition, t=0.5) → frame at 0.5, and so on. Suddenly you have K times more training data from each trajectory. You're also free from the rollout error accumulation—each prediction is directly from the initial condition, not chained predictions. And you can evaluate at any time, not just grid points. The trade-off is that your network is now more intricate: it has to learn time-conditioned operations at every layer. But the data advantage—having K independent training pairs per trajectory instead of K-1 sequential pairs in rollout—often wins out in practice, especially when data is expensive (which it always is in scientific computing).
key_ideas: Time-dependent problems come naturally as trajectories (videos, sequences)—the data has an intrinsic time direction—but standard operators were built to ignore time and just predict one final snapshot.

Rollout (autoregressive evaluation) is the naive fix: train one operator to predict the next frame, then apply it repeatedly. It works but accumulates errors, can't do continuous time, and wastes trajectory information by only using sequential pairs.

Error accumulation happens because small errors compound over many steps, and the network drifts into regimes it was never trained on. Backpropagating through 50+ steps also causes vanishing/exploding gradients during training.
Time conditioning makes time explicit as an input to the neural operator, so the network learns to output different solutions for different times given the same initial condition.

Conditional normalization (applying time-dependent transformation at every layer's normalization) keeps time information alive deep in the network, instead of letting it be forgotten after the first few layers.
Time-conditioned networks extract K times more training pairs from each trajectory (one pair per time point, not just sequential pairs), which is a huge data advantage when simulations are expensive.
The approach is general: any architecture that uses normalization (convolution, transformers, etc.) can be conditioned on time by modifying how normalization works in each layer.
u1KFcAvjyCI.worked_intuition: Let's make this concrete with a heat equation. Suppose you simulate heat diffusing through a metal rod and save 10 frames. Old approach: train operator_0 on (initial, frame_5), operator_5 on (initial, frame_10), etc.—separate models. Rollout approach: train one model on (frame_i, frame_{i+1}) pairs—so (frame_0, frame_1), (frame_1, frame_2), ..., (frame_9, frame_10)—and at test time, feed the output back in. Problem: frame_1 prediction has 1% error, frame_2 now has error from both steps, by frame_10 the heat distribution is completely wrong. Time-conditioning approach: train one model that takes (initial, time=0.1) and outputs frame_1, (initial, time=0.2) and outputs frame_2, ..., (initial, time=1.0) and outputs frame_10. Now you have 10 independent training examples from one trajectory. At test time, you just ask the network 'given this initial condition, what's the heat at time=0.47?' and it answers directly, no chaining, no error accumulation. The network learns internally that temperature diffuses smoothly over time, and time-conditioned normalization ensures that at each layer, the representation is adapted for the time you're querying.
u1KFcAvjyCI.where_it_breaks: Time conditioning assumes you can condition every layer's normalization on time, which works well for architectures with built-in normalization (convnets with batch-norm, transformers with layer-norm). For architectures without normalization or with atypical designs, the trick needs adaptation. Also, the approach assumes you have the full trajectory for each training example—if your data only gives you pairs (initial, final) without intermediate frames, time conditioning gives back some but not all of the data advantage. On very long trajectories (predicting 1000 steps into the future), even with time conditioning, you're asking the network to extrapolate far beyond its training range, which can break down if the system has transients or instabilities. The method also assumes uniform spacing in time for simplicity—non-uniform sampling requires a bit more care. And like all neural networks, generalization to new initial conditions or parameters depends on training diversity; if your initial conditions are all drawn from one narrow regime, the network won't extrapolate well to others.
u1KFcAvjyCI.takeaway: Time-dependent neural operators should take time as an explicit input, conditioning every layer on time through normalization, rather than hiding time and using rollout. This avoids error accumulation, enables continuous-time prediction, and multiplies your effective training data by the trajectory length. It's a small architectural change with a large practical payoff.

wBNYF7tpvaw.plain_title: What Neural Networks Are and How to Train Them with Data
wBNYF7tpvaw.big_question: How can we learn the physics of a system (captured by differential equations) from data using neural networks? What is actually happening inside a neural network, and why are they so hard to train?
wBNYF7tpvaw.everyday_anchor: Imagine neurons in your brain as tiny decision-makers: they receive signals, weigh them, and decide whether to pass a message along. A neural network mimics this by stacking these simple decision units—each one doing a tiny bit of work, but together learning to predict temperature from pressure, or motion from forces.
walkthrough: The story of neural networks starts in 1943 with McCulloch and Pitts, who realized something remarkable: the brain's neurons could be captured in math as simple logical devices. Each biological neuron collects electrical inputs, weighs them through chemical channels, and fires (or doesn't) based on whether a threshold is crossed. They abstracted this into the threshold logic unit—a single number that takes multiple inputs (x1, x2, etc.), multiplies each by a weight (w1, w2), adds a bias term, and then applies a threshold step function. This was not meant to be biologically perfect; it was a massive simplification. But it worked mathematically. The genius move came in 1957 when Rosenblatt realized these weights didn't have to be fixed—they could be learned from data. This learning capacity was the birth of the modern perceptron.

When you stack many of these simple units together in layers, you get a neural network (also called a multi-layer perceptron or MLP). Here's the structure: you take an input (say, a vector of numbers describing a system's state), pass it through a layer that multiplies by weights and adds bias—this is called an affine transformation, borrowing from geometry. Then you apply a scalar nonlinearity (a function applied element-by-element, like ReLU or hyperbolic tangent) that introduces the essential nonlinearity. You repeat this affine-then-nonlinearity pattern layer after layer. The output is your prediction. The whole thing is just a mathematical function: given input, produce output. But it's a parametric function—its behavior depends entirely on the weights and biases. Change those parameters and you have a completely different function.

The activation function (the nonlinearity) is crucial. Early networks used the Heaviside step function—inspired directly by thresholds in biology. But this turns out to be terrible for learning: its gradient (the slope, used for optimization) is zero almost everywhere. Instead, modern networks use smooth approximations like sigmoid (which looks S-shaped) or hyperbolic tangent. The most popular choice today is ReLU—rectified linear unit—which simply keeps positive values and zeros out negative ones. ReLU is fast and works well, but it has a kink (the gradient jumps from zero to one), which is why variants like Leaky ReLU exist. The choice of activation matters somewhat, but the deeper secret is that almost any smooth nonlinear activation function will work. The universal approximation theorem tells us something profound: any continuous function (describing any physics you care about) can be approximated arbitrarily closely using a neural network with just one hidden layer, as long as it has the right weights and bias.

But here's the million-dollar question: how do we find those weights? This is where supervised learning comes in. You don't have access to the ground truth function f(y) that governs your system everywhere. Instead, you probe the system at N sample points y₁, y₂, etc.—imagine running experiments or simulations—and measure the output (with a bit of noise added by measurement error). This creates a labeled dataset: input-output pairs. Your task is to find weights such that when you feed these input points into the neural network, the predicted outputs match the measured outputs as closely as possible. You quantify 'closeness' with a loss function—typically the L2 norm (mean squared error), which sums the squared differences between prediction and truth across all data points. The goal of training is to minimize this loss by adjusting the weights.

This minimization problem is deceptively hard. First, the parameter space is enormous. Even a small neural network has thousands of parameters (weights and biases). Large practical networks have millions or billions. This means you're trying to minimize a function in a space with billions of dimensions. Second, and worse, the loss landscape is hideously non-convex. If it were convex (like a simple valley), you could guarantee finding the global minimum. But neural networks are non-convex because of the layered affine-nonlinearity structure. The composition of nonlinear functions creates a landscape full of valleys, ridges, and saddle points. You might get stuck in a local minimum—a place where every direction uphill looks worse, even though a much better solution exists elsewhere.

To solve this, almost everyone uses gradient descent. The idea is simple: compute the gradient (the direction of steepest descent), take a step down that direction, repeat. In pure form, you'd compute the loss across all N data points, then move your parameters. But this is slow and memory-hungry for large datasets. So in practice, people use stochastic gradient descent (SGD): pick a single data point or a small batch, compute the approximate gradient from that tiny sample, and step. This is a poor approximation of the true gradient, but it's much faster. The trade-off is noisier, more erratic progress—sometimes you move the wrong way. But with enough steps and a properly tuned learning rate (how big each step is), you can still converge to a reasonably good solution, not necessarily the global minimum but a local one that generalizes well.

The learning rate is critical and finicky. Too large and you overshoot and oscillate wildly. Too small and training crawls. This is why training neural networks feels like an art: practitioners learn tricks like warm-up schedules, adaptive learning rates (algorithms like Adam that adjust step size per parameter), and careful initialization of weights. Early in training, you have random, terrible weights, so the loss is huge. As you train, the loss drops—the network learns to fit the data. But there's a danger: the network can memorize the training data perfectly without learning general patterns, a problem called overfitting. You need a validation set to catch this. In the context of physics-informed machine learning, this is particularly important because we care about generalizing beyond the probe points we measured.
key_ideas: A neural network is a parametric function built from layers of affine transformations (multiply-weight-add-bias) followed by scalar nonlinearities (element-wise application of functions like ReLU). By composing many such layers, the network gains the capacity to approximate any continuous function (universal approximation theorem).

Training a neural network means finding weights and biases that minimize a loss function—the mismatch between the network's predictions and the measured data. This is solved iteratively using gradient descent, computing which direction decreases loss most steeply and stepping that way.

The optimization landscape is non-convex and high-dimensional. Gradient descent often gets trapped in local minima and is sensitive to the learning rate (step size). In practice, stochastic gradient descent uses small batches of data per step, trading computational speed for noisy, erratic progress.

Activation functions like ReLU (keep positives, zero negatives) introduce nonlinearity. They are essential: without them, stacking affine layers would collapse into a single affine layer. Different activations exist, but the main requirement is smoothness (or at least non-polynomial behavior) for universal approximation.
wBNYF7tpvaw.worked_intuition: Consider fitting a temperature profile to airflow data over an airfoil (airplane wing shape). You run simulations at different airfoil geometries and measure drag, lift, pressure. You have 100 probe points. A shallow neural network might look like: input (24 airfoil parameters) → 50 hidden neurons with ReLU → 3 output neurons (drag, lift, pressure). The hidden layer computes 50 weighted combinations of the 24 inputs, then applies ReLU (zero out negatives), then a final affine layer maps those 50 ReLU outputs to your 3 quantities. Training starts with random weights. You compute loss: average squared error between predicted and true (drag, lift, pressure). Gradient descent steepens on this landscape: which weight change reduces loss most? Adjust weights slightly in that direction. Repeat thousands of times. Eventually, the network learns which combinations of input geometry matter for each output.
wBNYF7tpvaw.where_it_breaks: The universal approximation theorem guarantees a neural network exists to fit any continuous function, but it's silent on three real obstacles. First, the proof is non-constructive—it doesn't tell you how many neurons you need or what weights to use. Second, finding those weights via gradient descent on non-convex loss is hard: you may converge to a local minimum far from optimal. Third, overfitting: the network may memorize training data without learning the underlying pattern, failing on new probe points. Additionally, this theory assumes access to plenty of labeled data; with only three measurements (as the lecturer mentions), modern neural networks are not reliable. The theory also assumes the true function is continuous, but physics can have discontinuities or bifurcations. Finally, computing gradients for billion-parameter networks is expensive: you need GPUs and distributed computing.
wBNYF7tpvaw.takeaway: A neural network is a stack of simple affine-nonlinearity pairs (layers) that forms a parametric function. You find the right weights by minimizing a loss function using gradient descent, which is easy to understand but deceptively hard in practice because the landscape is non-convex and high-dimensional. The main miracle is that even with this difficulty, the simple compositional structure—matrix multiply, add bias, apply ReLU, repeat—turns out to be effective enough to learn physics from data. But you'll need a reasonable amount of clean data, careful tuning of hyperparameters (learning rate, network size), and patience to make it work.

wJSgLRiU7D4.plain_title: Attention as a learned, data-dependent kernel for scientific fields
wJSgLRiU7D4.big_question: How can we use Transformers (which were designed for language) to learn operators that map scientific fields to other fields, and how do we make them computationally feasible when your data lives on a high-resolution grid?
wJSgLRiU7D4.everyday_anchor: Imagine you're trying to predict the temperature at one point in a room. You could look at all other points and decide which ones matter most—nearby points matter more, far ones less. Attention does exactly this, but lets the machine *learn* which points matter, and learns it differently depending on the data it sees. Most other approaches bake in a fixed rule (like "nearby is important"), but attention figures it out from scratch.
walkthrough: At its heart, a Transformer is a stack of blocks that look at relationships between different parts of your input. The key piece is *attention*, which is a way to compute "which other parts of my input should I focus on when computing the output at this location?" You have input points (let's call them tokens—think of them as grid points in your domain), and for each token you ask: what weighted combination of all the other tokens should I use? The weight for each other token is computed by a softmax, which just means: how important is this other token, as a probability that sums to 1. The clever part is that these weights are learned—they're not hard-coded. If your data has a lot of local structure, the network will learn to give high weight to nearby points and low weight to distant ones. But if your problem needs global information, the network can learn that too.

Here's why this is different from other operator learners like CNNs or Fourier Neural Operators. A CNN uses a *fixed kernel*—you decide in advance that a point depends only on its 3×3 neighbors, and this kernel is the same everywhere and doesn't change based on the data. Fourier Neural Operators learn a kernel in Fourier space, but again it's fixed once trained. Attention builds a *data-dependent kernel*. Every point can in principle attend to every other point, and the strength of that attention is learned from the data. This is wildly more flexible, but it comes at a cost: you have to compute attention weights between all pairs of points, which is *quadratic* in the number of points.

Let's make that cost concrete. Imagine a simple incompressible fluid in 2D. At each grid point you have 2 values (the x and y components of velocity). If your domain is 128 × 128, that's 2^14 grid points. The attention calculation scales as (2^14)^2 = 2^28 operations—that's roughly a billion. Now move to 3D at the same resolution: 128^3 = 2^21 points, so 2^42 operations—trillions. Your computer can't handle this. And you're doing this not just once at inference (when you use the trained model), but thousands of times during training, looping over your entire dataset.

The solution for images is *patching*. Instead of treating each pixel as a token, you group nearby pixels into patches—say 16×16. A 128×128 image becomes just 64 tokens (one per patch). You learn a small neural network that extracts features from each patch—a weighted average with learnable weights—and feeds these 64 learned summaries into the Transformer. Now the quadratic cost is on 64 tokens instead of 2^14, which is 4096 instead of 268 million operations. The trade-off: you lose fine-grained information when you average pixels into a patch. The fix: you learn additional feature channels (like you increase from 2 to 20 dimensions) so the network can recover detail.

But here's the rub for scientific fields: if you're predicting temperature or stress at each point, a 16×16 patch loses too much. You might need 4×4 or 8×8 patches to capture the physics. A 4×4 patch multiplies the number of tokens by 16, which multiplies the quadratic cost by 256—suddenly you're back to infeasibility. The paper introduces *windowed attention* to solve this. Instead of computing attention across all patches, you divide your domain into larger windows (say, 4×4 windows, each containing 4×4 patches). Inside each window, patches attend only to each other—like a CNN's receptive field. This cuts the quadratic cost dramatically: if you have 20 windows instead of 256 patches, 20^2 = 400 operations instead of 256^2 = 65,536.

The remaining trick is that you *shift* the windows across layers. In layer 1, your window partitions the domain one way. In layer 2, you shift the partition—so a pair of patches that were in different windows in layer 1 are now in the same window. By alternating the window positions, information slowly propagates globally. After a few layers, even patches that were far apart initially have been brought into the same attention window, so they influence each other. It's like a CNN's receptive field growing with depth, but done via discrete shifts instead of strides.

To wrap up: attention is a learned, fully data-driven way to decide which parts of your input contribute to the output at each location. This is effective—it can discover both local and global structure—but expensive. For scientific fields on grids, you patch to compress tokens, then use windowed attention to avoid the full quadratic cost. You trade off some information loss (from patching) for computational feasibility, but you recover it by learning richer features in the compressed patches. The key intuition is that attention without constraints is too expensive, so you impose structure (patches, windows, shifts) that respects the regularity of physical fields—things change slowly locally, but accumulate change over large distances.
key_ideas: Attention is a learned kernel (not fixed like CNNs): each point learns to weight all others based on the data, so it can discover whether locality, global reach, or a hybrid is important.
Quadratic cost: Attention requires comparing every pair of tokens, which scales as (number of tokens)^2—OK for text (thousands of tokens), infeasible for grids (millions+).
Patching: Group grid points into patches, extract learned features per patch (weighted averages), reducing tokens from millions to thousands, quadratic cost from trillions to millions.
Windowed attention: Compute attention only within local windows, not globally; shift windows across layers so distant patches eventually interact, keeping cost linear or log-linear.
Information loss vs. computation: Patching loses detail, but you recover it by learning more feature channels per patch—trading spatial resolution for channel depth.
Data-dependent inductive bias: Unlike CNNs (which bake in locality) or FNOs (fixed Fourier kernel), attention learns its inductive biases from data, so it can adapt to different physics.
wJSgLRiU7D4.worked_intuition: Consider predicting velocity in a 2D fluid from pressure. Without any structure, pure attention on a 128×128 grid is infeasible (2^28 ops). You patch to 64 patches (cost now ~4000 ops). But 16×16 patches might smear out shear flows at the boundaries. You shrink to 8×8 patches (256 tokens, ~65k ops)—still expensive but doable. Now you add windowed attention: group 256 patches into 16 windows of 16 patches each. In layer 1, each window attends internally (16^2 = 256 ops per window, 16 windows total = 4k ops). In layer 2, shift the windows so different pairs overlap. After 4–5 layers of shifted windows, any two original patches have been co-attended. The model learns that nearby patches contribute strongly (via high attention weights) and distant ones weakly (learned by the network), so it approximates locality without hard-coding it. The network also discovers if there are long-range correlations (e.g., a faraway pressure anomaly that triggers flow at your point) because after shifting, all pairs eventually interact.
wJSgLRiU7D4.where_it_breaks: Windowed attention loses global information within a single layer—you can't see across the domain at once. If your physics has strong long-range correlations (e.g., a shock wave that couples distant regions instantly), you need many layers of window-shifts to propagate information, which increases depth and training time. Patching itself loses high-frequency detail; if your problem has sharp gradients or thin boundary layers, a 4×4 or 8×8 patch is still coarse. The network tries to recover this via learned feature channels, but there's a hard limit: if the patch size is too large, you can't reconstruct sub-patch variation. Also, the approach assumes your domain is regular and patched regularly—it's less natural for unstructured meshes or irregular geometries. Finally, window shifts are discrete; information propagation is slow compared to global attention, so you need deep networks.
wJSgLRiU7D4.takeaway: Attention learns which parts of your input matter for the output, without hard-coding locality—effective but expensive on grids. Patching + windowed attention + shifts make it feasible: you compress the grid into tokens, attend locally to keep cost down, and shift windows across layers so information gradually propagates globally. The trade-off is simplicity for expressiveness, and you pay with depth and training time. It's a data-driven way to discover the right balance between local and global structure, which is why it works well when you don't know the physics a priori.

xoaMZJcd28M.plain_title: How to Solve Physics Equations Using Neural Networks
xoaMZJcd28M.big_question: Can we teach neural networks to solve physics equations (like the heat equation or fluid flow) without needing lots of solved examples?
xoaMZJcd28M.everyday_anchor: Imagine you want to find the temperature everywhere in a room over time. The traditional way (finite difference method) requires a huge grid of points and becomes impossible in many dimensions. But what if instead you trained a neural network to 'know' the physics law directly?
walkthrough: Let's start with the gap that inspired this whole approach. Standard machine learning works like image classification: you show a neural network millions of pictures labeled 'dog' or 'cat', and it learns to recognize. But physics problems are different. When you want to solve the heat equation (which governs how temperature spreads), you only know three things: (1) the initial temperature everywhere, (2) the boundary conditions (like what happens at the walls), and (3) the physical law itself—the equation that temperature satisfies. You do NOT have interior measurements showing what the temperature is at arbitrary points in the room. So there's a mismatch: standard machine learning demands labeled data at sample points, but physics-based problems only give you the equation and boundary values.

Here's the key insight that solves this puzzle: we can use the PDE (partial differential equation) itself as training signal. A partial differential equation is a mathematical rule that the true solution must satisfy everywhere. For instance, the heat equation says 'the time-derivative of temperature equals the space-derivative of temperature.' If we have a neural network that predicts temperature at any location and time, we can check: does this network actually satisfy the heat equation? To check, we compute the time-derivative of the network's output (using automatic differentiation—the backprop machinery), compute the spatial derivatives (also using backprop), and see if they match the equation. When they don't match, that mismatch is an error signal we can minimize.

Let's unpack what 'residual' means, because it's the engine of the whole method. A residual is the amount by which the equation is violated. If the true solution satisfies 'ut = uxx' perfectly, then substituting the neural network in gives some leftover term—that's the residual. We compute residuals at many random points scattered throughout the space-time domain. We also compute how badly the network fails to match the initial conditions (the temporal boundary) and spatial boundary conditions. These three types of mismatch—interior residual (PDE violation), initial condition error, and boundary condition error—are packaged into one loss function.

To make this practical, we face an immediate problem: the loss function involves integrals (summing error over the entire domain), and you can't compute integrals by hand. The solution is quadrature rules—numerical integration tricks that replace an integral with a weighted sum over sample points. The simplest is Monte Carlo: pick random points in the space-time domain and at the boundaries, evaluate the residuals and boundary errors at those points, then average them. More sophisticated quadrature (Gauss-Legendre, quasi-Monte Carlo) can do better, but the principle is the same: replace the integral with a finite weighted sum.

Now the algorithm is simple: (1) Choose some random collocation points (sampling points) throughout space-time and on boundaries. (2) Set up a neural network with random weights (just like for any neural network). (3) At each collocation point, compute the residual of the PDE using automatic differentiation. (4) At each boundary point, compute how far the network is from satisfying the boundary condition. (5) Sum all these errors into a loss function. (6) Use gradient descent (Adam, LBFGS, or any optimizer) to minimize this loss. If training succeeds, the network weights adjust until the residuals vanish—meaning the network has learned a function that satisfies the PDE and boundary conditions.

Why is this remarkable? First, you don't need any ground-truth solution samples. The PDE itself is your training signal. Second, the method is almost trivial to code: once you have automatic differentiation (which any deep learning approach provides), computing derivatives with respect to space/time is no harder than computing derivatives with respect to network weights. Computing the residual of a nonlinear PDE is just composing automatic differentiation calls. Third, the method scales to high dimensions much better than traditional grid-based methods. In grid methods, if you need 100 grid points per spatial dimension, then in 5D you need 100^5 = 10 billion points—intractable. With neural networks and random collocation points, you just pick more points as dimension increases; there's no exponential grid explosion.

Let's see how far this reaches. For linear PDEs like the heat equation, it works beautifully: even in 100 dimensions, you get ~1% error. For nonlinear PDEs like Burgers equation (which combines transport with diffusion), it works too—the network learns to capture the sharp fronts and smooth regions. For the Navier-Stokes equations (which govern fluid flow), the network outputs a vector (velocity field) instead of a scalar, and the same residual logic applies: check that the momentum equations and continuity equation are satisfied. Even for higher-order PDEs with third or fifth derivatives (like the KdV equation with solitons), automatic differentiation just keeps applying the chain rule. The method generalizes because it's fundamentally agnostic about which equation you're solving—just give it the equation form, and it builds the residual.

But there are real limitations. When you have many higher-order derivatives, automatic differentiation becomes expensive and accumulates numerical error. The loss landscape becomes nonconvex, so gradient descent can get stuck in local minima and fail to find a good solution. Enforcing boundary and initial conditions is soft (via the loss term), not hard, so unless the loss term has high weight, the learned solution can violate them slightly. The method assumes the solution is smooth; if shocks (true discontinuities) arise, neural networks smooth over them. And for inverse problems (inferring the equation from noisy data), the method becomes sensitive to noise. These aren't dealbreakers, but they explain why PINNs succeed in some regimes and struggle in others.
key_ideas: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs): A neural network trained to satisfy a PDE by minimizing the residual (the equation violation) rather than matching data samples.
Residual as training signal: Instead of labeled ground truth, the PDE itself becomes the loss function—measure how badly the equation is violated at sample points, and minimize that.

Automatic differentiation for both inputs and parameters: The same backprop machinery that computes weight gradients can compute spatial/temporal derivatives of the network output, making it cheap to evaluate residuals.
Collocation points and quadrature: Replace integrals with weighted sums over randomly sampled points in space-time, turning continuous optimization into a finite sum.
Dimension advantage: Unlike grid-based methods that explode exponentially with dimensions, PINNs use scattered points, so high-dimensional PDEs (50D, 100D) become tractable.
