Generality across equation types: The method works for linear, nonlinear, scalar, vector, first-order, second-order, and higher-order PDEs—just change the equation form, same code.
Hard vs soft constraints: Boundary and initial conditions are enforced softly in the loss (can be violated slightly) rather than hard-coded, which is simpler but less rigid.
xoaMZJcd28M.worked_intuition: Consider the heat equation ut = uxx in 1D space with zero boundary conditions. Start with a fully-connected neural network u_theta(x,t) with random weights theta. Evaluate it at, say, 1000 random (x,t) points inside the domain and 100 points on the boundary x=0 and x=1. At each interior point, use PyTorch autodiff to compute du/dt and d²u/dx², then form residual = du/dt - d²u/dx². At each boundary point, compute u_theta(0,t) and u_theta(1,t)—these should be zero. At t=0, compute u_theta(x,0) and compare to the initial condition. Now form loss = mean(residual²) + 10*mean(boundary_error²) + 10*mean(ic_error²). Backprop this scalar loss to get gradients of theta, then one step of Adam or SGD. Repeat for thousands of iterations. As the loss shrinks, the network gradually learns weights that make du/dt ≈ d²u/dx², boundaries ≈ 0, and initial condition ≈ given. At convergence, evaluating u_theta at any new (x,t) gives an approximation to the true heat equation solution.
xoaMZJcd28M.where_it_breaks: PINNs struggle when solutions are truly discontinuous (shocks in fluid dynamics)—neural networks smooth over discontinuities, so you get 5-10% error instead of 1%. Computing many high-order derivatives via autodiff becomes numerically unstable and expensive. If the PDE is stiff or has widely different timescales, gradient descent gets slow or trapped in local minima. Inverse problems (inferring equation parameters from noisy measurement data) are sensitive: noise in the data propagates through the residual and corrupts learned solutions. For very intricate geometries with intricate boundaries, enforcing boundary conditions softly via loss weighting is crude compared to hard-constraint methods. The method also assumes smoothness; it cannot easily encode conservation laws as hard constraints the way structured discretizations can.
xoaMZJcd28M.takeaway: Neural networks can solve PDEs without solving examples—by treating the equation violation (the residual) as a loss function and letting automatic differentiation compute derivatives. This flips the usual machine learning approach from data-driven to physics-driven, and it scales to high dimensions where traditional numerical methods fail. But it trades rigor for flexibility: boundary conditions are soft, discontinuities are smeared, and you're always finding a local optimum of the residual, not necessarily the true global solution.

yhHhMmiNl_g.plain_title: Learning to Solve Differential Equations as Opaque model Transformations
yhHhMmiNl_g.big_question: How can we teach a machine learning model to predict the solution to a differential equation without physically solving it, when the inputs and outputs are both infinite-dimensional functions rather than fixed-size numbers?
yhHhMmiNl_g.everyday_anchor: Imagine you have a physical simulator (like a weather model or aerodynamic design tool) that takes a description of initial conditions or design parameters and outputs a intricate flow pattern. Running that simulator even once takes hours. Can you train a neural network to act like that simulator, so that after you've run it a few times, the network can instantly predict new outputs without the expensive computation?
walkthrough: At its heart, solving a differential equation (a PDE) is a transformation: it takes inputs—like material properties, source terms, or initial conditions—and produces outputs, which are solutions spread across space and time. The key insight is that these inputs and outputs are not single numbers; they are functions. A function is something defined at every point in space, so it cannot be fully captured by a finite list of numbers. When you describe a function, you need infinite information. Because of this fundamental fact, solving a PDE is really about learning an operator: a machine that takes a function as input and produces a function as output. This is fundamentally different from a standard neural network, which takes a finite list of numbers and outputs another finite list.

To see why this matters, consider a simple advection equation: if you start with some initial shape (a function of space) and let it move at constant velocity, the solution is just that shape shifted by a distance. The operator here is the 'shifting' operation. It takes any input function (like sine wave, exponential, or a square bump) and produces the shifted version. The remarkable part is that the same operator works for all possible input functions—it is universal in that sense. But because the input is infinite-dimensional (a full function), the operator must also handle infinite-dimensional output. You cannot describe a function using only ten numbers; you need it fully specified to capture all its details.

Now, how do you actually train a machine learning model on this? The practical trick is what the lecturer calls 'cheating.' Instead of trying to learn the operator on all possible functions (which is impossible), you restrict the problem. For instance, in aircraft wing design, you don't consider arbitrary wing shapes. Instead, you specify that any design is built by adjusting maybe twenty to fifty parameters—like thickness at different points along the wing—starting from a reference shape. Suddenly, your input becomes finite-dimensional: it is just those twenty to fifty numbers. Similarly, you can restrict your outputs: instead of predicting the full fluid flow everywhere, you might predict pressure at specific points or overall quantities like lift and drag. With this restriction, the problem transforms from 'infinite-to-infinite' into something like 'finite-to-finite,' and now you can use standard deep neural networks.

Once you have restricted the problem this way, the training procedure is straightforward. You randomly generate many design parameters within the allowed range (say, one thousand different wing designs). For each, you run an expensive simulation (perhaps an aerodynamic solver taking one to two minutes per run) and record the outputs. After you have collected this dataset—pairing each set of input parameters with its resulting solution—you train a neural network to predict the outputs given the inputs. The network learns the relationship by fitting to your data using standard stochastic gradient descent. From the mathematician's perspective, this works because universal approximation theorems guarantee that a neural network can learn any continuous mapping, given enough capacity and data. The map from finite-dimensional inputs to finite-dimensional outputs is a standard machine learning problem.

However, there is a price. Even though approximation error—the error from the network's inability to represent the true solution exactly—is not the main bottleneck (solutions to PDEs have useful structure and regularity that allows neural networks to learn them efficiently), the generalization error is. When your training data is drawn randomly, the gap between how well the network performs on seen data and unseen data is roughly inversely proportional to the square root of the number of samples. This square-root dependence is brutal when your single simulation takes minutes to hours. If you want 1% accuracy and your data varies over a range of, say, 100, then you need the square-root of your sample size to be 100, meaning you need 10,000 samples. If each sample costs 2 minutes of computation, that is 20,000 minutes—more than two weeks of continuous computing. In three-dimensional problems, a single simulation can take hours or even days, making this completely infeasible.

This is the core challenge the lecture poses: we live in a data-poor regime. Unlike the big-data success stories of modern machine learning (where billions of images or text samples are available), scientific computing offers perhaps hundreds of simulations—not thousands or millions. The 'cheating' approach breaks down precisely because you cannot afford to generate enough training data. The gap between what the theory says you need (10,000 samples) and what you can realistically afford (maybe 100 or 1,000) is the chasm that the rest of the course will address. The question becomes: how do you use machine learning when data is expensive and scarce, not abundant?

Understanding the operator perspective is the entry point to this challenge. By recognizing that PDEs are input-output transformations operating on functions, we can think clearly about what it means to approximate them. The restriction to finite dimensions—the 'cheating'—makes the problem tractable in principle but reveals the real bottleneck: data efficiency. Moving forward, the course will explore ways to use physics-based constraints, symmetries, and other structural properties to learn operators from relatively few expensive simulations.
key_ideas: Operators are input-output transformations on infinite-dimensional spaces (functions): Unlike neural networks that map fixed-size numerical inputs to fixed-size numerical outputs, PDEs map full functions (defined everywhere in space) to other full functions. These transformations are called operators.

Solving a PDE is equivalent to learning the operator: Finding the solution to a PDE given some input parameters (material properties, initial conditions, etc.) is the same as learning the operator that transforms inputs to outputs. This reframes PDE solving as a machine learning task.

The finite-dimensional restriction or 'cheating': You make the problem tractable by assuming your inputs belong to a restricted class (parameterized by finitely many numbers), like wing designs defined by twenty parameters. This converts the infinite-dimensional operator learning problem into a standard finite-dimensional regression task that deep neural networks can handle.

Universal approximation provides a theoretical guarantee: Theorems guarantee that shallow neural networks can approximate any continuous mapping to arbitrary precision. This means that in principle, the network can learn to approximate the operator—but only if you have enough data and training capacity.

Sample difficulty and the square-root barrier: The generalization error (gap between training and test performance) scales roughly as inverse square-root of the number of samples. This means you need many samples to achieve high accuracy, which is catastrophic when each sample requires an expensive simulation—often 10,000+ samples when you can only afford 100 to 1,000.

Data poverty is the binding constraint: Science and engineering have the opposite problem from Internet-scale machine learning. You have scarce, expensive data (simulations taking minutes to hours each) rather than abundant cheap data (like photos). This regime requires fundamentally different strategies than standard deep learning.
yhHhMmiNl_g.worked_intuition: Imagine you are designing an airplane wing. A wing's shape is described by its profile at each position—but you could specify it using just twenty parameters (thickness here, curve there, angle elsewhere). Now, for a given wing (specified by those twenty numbers), you want to predict the air pressure distribution around it and ultimately the lift and drag. Running a fluid simulator once takes 2 minutes. You run it on, say, 200 random wing designs and collect 200 data points pairing each design (twenty numbers) with its pressure field and performance (twenty outputs, say: lift, drag, and eighteen pressure values at key points). Now you train a neural network: input the twenty design parameters, the network predicts the twenty outputs. The network learns the pattern from your 200 examples. Once trained, predicting a new design takes milliseconds instead of two minutes. This works because the network has learned a smooth approximation to the relationship between designs and their aerodynamic behavior. However, if you wanted higher accuracy (say, to predict 500 pressure values instead of 18), you would need a lot more training data—perhaps thousands of expensive simulations. This is the bottleneck: the operator (the true relationship between wing shape and airflow) requires many samples to learn accurately when data is costly.
yhHhMmiNl_g.where_it_breaks: The approach breaks down in three ways. First, if your restricted input space does not actually contain the solutions you care about (e.g., your wing design parameters cannot represent the optimal shape), the network cannot learn to find it, no matter how much data you have. Second, if you want high accuracy on the full field solution (not just a few summary numbers), the output becomes very high-dimensional, and you need even more data—the curse of dimensionality. Third, and most fundamentally, the data cost is prohibitive: achieving 1% error on a realistic aerodynamics problem might require 10,000 simulations; if each costs one hour, that is more than a year of computing. Scientific problems are data-poor by nature. The next lectures address this by using physics-based constraints and structure to learn operators with far fewer samples than the naive 'neural network on restricted inputs' approach requires.
yhHhMmiNl_g.takeaway: Solving a PDE is fundamentally an operator learning problem: you are learning an input-output transformation on infinite-dimensional function spaces. The practical trick of restricting to finite dimensions lets you use standard neural networks, but it reveals the real constraint: you need expensive simulations, so your data is sparse. This incompatibility between the statistical sample difficulty required and the computational budget available is the core challenge that motivates data-efficient operator learning methods.

z3tQaNOwQqM.plain_title: Why Neural Networks Struggle to Learn Deep Patterns, and How to Fix It
z3tQaNOwQqM.big_question: If neural networks are universal approximators that can learn any function, why do they fail on real problems? And what practical tricks actually make them work?
z3tQaNOwQqM.everyday_anchor: Imagine teaching someone to recognize faces from photographs. A bad strategy is to show them just 9 photos and expect them to recognize anyone. A good strategy adds three things: (1) show them lots of different photos, (2) gently guide the learning—don't let them memorize the details of those 9—and (3) use better learning methods than just pointing 'go in the direction of the error.' That's what this lecture is about.
walkthrough: Neural networks are just functions. We start with some inputs (like pixels), pass them through a mathematical function that depends on many parameters (weights), and get outputs (like a predicted category). The simplest approach is to take all your labeled training data, create a loss function that measures how wrong the network is, and use gradient descent—repeatedly nudging the weights downhill—to train it. That's the recipe. But in practice, three major problems block your way to a working network, and they are worth understanding one by one.

The first problem is underfitting and overfitting: a fundamental tension between model size and generalization. Imagine fitting a polynomial curve to data. If your polynomial is linear (degree 1), it fits poorly because it is too simple—high bias, low variance. If your polynomial has degree 100, it might fit your training data perfectly but wildly oscillates between points and fails on new data—low bias, high variance. The same tension appears with neural networks: a small network underfits; a large network overfits. This is NOT a flaw in the theory. It is because (1) you only have finite training data, not the entire true distribution (estimation error), and (2) your network architecture may not be expressive enough to capture the true function (approximation error). To navigate this, you can increase the model difficulty if you are underfitting, or add more training data, use regularization techniques (adding soft constraints to prefer simpler solutions), or apply early stopping (halt training before the network starts memorizing noise).

The second major problem is optimization error: even if your network is the right size, the loss landscape is incredibly rugged and high-dimensional, full of local minima and flat plateaus. Vanilla gradient descent gets stuck in local minima by following the gradient downhill—it has no mechanism to escape. But there are clever tricks. Batch normalization (a layer that normalizes intermediate outputs to a fixed range) stabilizes training. Residual connections (skip connections that let gradients flow straight through a layer) allow deep networks to train by learning only the difference from the input instead of the full transformation. Xavier initialization (choosing weight starting values carefully) keeps layer outputs in a healthy range so gradients do not vanish. Weight regularization (penalizing large weights) encourages the network to learn compact, general features. Dropout (randomly disabling neurons during training) acts like an ensemble and prevents co-adaptation. These are not one-off hacks—they address fundamental mathematical issues in the loss landscape.

The third problem is the choice of optimizer. Standard gradient descent takes a fixed-size step in the gradient direction at each iteration. The Adam optimizer improves this in two ways: it maintains a running average of gradients (momentum), so if you are rolling downhill, you keep rolling even if the slope flattens, letting you escape shallow local minima; and it adapts the step size per parameter based on the magnitude of recent gradients, so parameters with small gradients take larger steps and vice versa. This makes Adam much more reliable than vanilla gradient descent, and it is the default choice in practice. Higher-order methods like Newton's method use second-derivative information (the Hessian matrix, which describes the local curvature) to take smarter steps, but computing the Hessian for a network with millions of parameters is prohibitively expensive, so approximations like L-BFGS are used selectively.

Regularization deserves deep attention because it is so central to making networks generalize. The core idea is to add extra terms to the loss function that discourage certain solutions. L2 regularization (penalizing large weights) comes from a Bayesian perspective: you assume a prior that weights are normally distributed around zero, so you are finding the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate rather than the maximum likelihood estimate. This mathematically encodes your belief that smaller weights are more plausible. More exotic regularizers can target frequencies (in image work, penalizing high-frequency components to keep predictions smooth), or operate in feature space (comparing network outputs not in pixel space but in the learned representation space of a pre-trained network). The key insight is that regularization does not change the model's hypothesis space—it does not shrink it. Instead, it prefers certain regions of the space over others. Data augmentation (rotating, cropping, or perturbing training images while keeping their labels) effectively grows your training set and naturally reduces overfitting. Self-supervised pre-training (training the network on a related unsupervised task first, like image reconstruction) gives it useful learned features that transfer to the main task. All of these fit the regularization approach: they guide the network away from memorization and toward generalization.

A concrete lesson from the loss landscape is spectral bias: fully-connected networks tend to learn low-frequency (smooth) patterns much faster than high-frequency (wiggly) patterns. This is actually a built-in regularizer—the network naturally learns a smooth approximation first, fitting the overall trend before memorizing noise. Early stopping uses this: if you stop training partway through, when training error and test error are both low, you capture a smooth model before overfitting begins. This is not magic—it is a consequence of the loss landscape's geometry and the way gradient descent explores it.

Finally, the lecture zooms out to show that Chat GPT itself, as impressive as it seems, is just this same recipe applied at massive scale. Chat GPT is trained to predict the next word in a sequence (an autoregressive task, a special case of classification). The input is a sequence of text tokens (words or sub-words), and the output is a probability distribution over the next word. The loss function is cross-entropy (the standard classification loss). The architecture is a Transformer: a deep neural network with 12 (or more) stacked blocks, each containing a feed-forward sub-network (just an MLP), residual connections, layer normalization (a variant of batch norm), and attention layers. Attention is the key innovation: for each word in the sequence, it learns a query vector; it compares that query to key vectors from all words in the sequence; and it computes attention weights (how much to 'look at' each word). These weights are then used to combine value vectors from all words, so each word is updated based on a weighted sum of all words. This mechanism lets the network model long-range relationships in text—e.g., recognizing that 'it' refers back to 'dog' many words earlier. Train this on billions of words from the internet and books, and from the simple task of predicting the next word, remarkable emergent abilities appear: Chat GPT can answer questions, translate, code, summarize, reason. Nothing new was added to the toolkit. The scale and data made the difference.

The takeaway is that modern neural network training is not a mystery. It is the interplay of three error sources—approximation, estimation, and optimization—each with concrete solutions. Use large enough networks (or better architectures like ResNets and Transformers) to express the target function. Add training data and regularization to prevent overfitting. Use good initialization, normalization, and optimizers (especially Adam) to navigate the loss landscape. Apply domain-specific tricks like attention for sequences. And scale it up. These techniques work across image classification, language modeling, scientific computing, and more. The magic is not in the theory—it is in the engineering of these pieces together.
key_ideas: Three sources of error: approximation (network not expressive enough), estimation (overfitting to finite training data), and optimization (getting stuck in bad local minima). Every practical technique targets one of these.
The bias-variance tradeoff is real: simple models underfit, intricate models overfit. Regularization biases the optimization toward simpler solutions without shrinking the hypothesis space.

Residual connections (x + f(x) instead of f(x)) allow deep networks to work because gradients can flow straight through a layer, bypassing the nonlinearity; the network learns to add a correction rather than learn the full mapping.
Batch normalization stabilizes training by normalizing layer outputs to a fixed range, preventing activation saturation and vanishing gradients caused by input/output scale mismatches.
Adam optimizer combines momentum (smoothed gradient history) and per-parameter adaptive step sizing, making it reliable to noise and local geometry changes in the loss landscape.

Attention is a sequence-to-sequence mechanism that learns which words to focus on when processing each word, enabling long-range reasoning in text and making Transformers effective for language tasks.

Chat GPT is just next-word prediction (a simple classification task) scaled to billions of words and parameters, with a Transformer architecture—remarkable abilities emerge from scale and data, not novel theory.
z3tQaNOwQqM.worked_intuition: Consider training a small network on MNIST digit recognition with only 9 training images (one of each digit plus a few duplicates). (1) Underfitting: a linear model fits poorly because it is too simple—it predicts most digits as a blurry average. Solution: add hidden layers. (2) But a network with 10,000 parameters trained on 9 images overfits badly—it memorizes each image exactly, learning spurious details (like the pen scratch on digit 3 in your sample) instead of the essence of 'digit 3'. Solutions: (a) add more training data (augment by rotating, shifting; or pre-train on a larger dataset); (b) regularize (penalize large weights, use dropout, early stop when test error starts rising); (c) use a ResNet with skip connections instead of a vanilla MLP, so gradients do not vanish in deep layers. (3) Even with a well-sized network and data, vanilla SGD with a fixed learning rate gets stuck. Switch to Adam: its momentum lets you escape a sharp local minimum, and its adaptive learning rate per parameter balances fast learning on some weights and careful learning on others. The combination works.
z3tQaNOwQqM.where_it_breaks: These techniques fail when: (1) the true function is outside the network's hypothesis space (e.g., training a neural network to learn a proof system from examples of theorems, when proof-checking is uncomputable—no architecture will help). (2) You have severe class imbalance or distribution shift: regularization assumes training and test data are i.i.d. from the same distribution; if test data come from a shifted distribution, your network generalizes poorly. (3) Scaling becomes infeasible: a network with 1 trillion parameters cannot be trained on a single machine, and distributed training introduces synchronization overhead and communication costs that worsen learning dynamics. (4) The loss landscape is not convex or even locally convex—many neural network loss functions have saddle points and plateaus where gradients are nearly zero, and no optimizer perfectly escapes these. (5) Regularization can hurt if applied too aggressively: a large L2 penalty may prevent the network from learning necessary difficulty. The art is in tuning.
z3tQaNOwQqM.takeaway: Neural networks are effective not because they are theoretically special, but because the engineering recipe (good initialization + normalization + regularization + a modern optimizer like Adam + enough data) works in practice. The three sources of error—approximation, estimation, optimization—each have concrete fixes, and combining them lets you train deep networks on real problems. Attention and Transformers extend this recipe to sequences. Scale it up (as in Chat GPT), and surprising emergent abilities appear.
